title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
國家任賢能以興治設科舉以取士
得士之多致治之盛誠近代之所
罕及欽惟
皇帝以上聖之資承
列聖之統嗣位以来日御
經筵講求二帝三王脩齊治平之道
===
以緝熈
聖學臨幸胄監祗謁
先聖崇重師道大新學政增廣科額
孜孜焉以旁求俊乂茂隆化理為
先務聲教漸被雖海隅僻遠之地
弦誦相聞天下學者莫不夙夜奮
勵圖以其業進售有司登用於朝布

會試錄序

國家任賢能以興治，設科舉以取士。得士之多，致治之盛，誠近代之所罕及。欽惟皇帝以上聖之資，承列聖之統，嗣位以来，日御經筵，講求二帝、三王脩齊治平之道，以緝熈聖學；臨幸胄監，祗謁先聖，崇重師道，大新學政，增廣科額，孜孜焉以旁求俊乂、茂隆化理為先務。聲教漸被，雖海隅僻遠之地，弦誦相聞。天下學者莫不夙夜奮勵，圖以其業進售有司，登用於朝，布
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

The state employs the worthy and capable to bring about good governance, and establishes the civil service examinations to select scholars. The abundance of scholars obtained and the flourishing of the governance achieved are truly rarely matched in recent eras. We reverently reflect that the Emperor, endowed with supreme sagehood, has inherited the succession of the line of Emperors. Since ascending the throne, he has daily attended the Classics Colloquium to investigate and seek out the Way of self-cultivation, family regulation, state governance, and world pacification of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, so as to continuously illumine his sagely learning. He has visited the Directorate of Education in person, reverently paid homage to the Former Sage, exalted the Way of the teacher, greatly renewed educational administration, and expanded the examination quotas, tirelessly making the wide search for eminent talent and the flourishing advancement of transformative governance his foremost task. As his prestigious teachings have gradually spread, even in remote corners by the sea the sounds of stringed instruments and chanting can be heard everywhere. Among scholars throughout the realm, there are none who do not rouse and exert themselves day and night, aspiring to present their scholarship to the authorities, ascend to employment at court, be placed in…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
列庶位盡瘁事
國仰副
聖心求賢輔治之誠是盖有虞黎獻共
臣之日成周多士濟濟之時猗歟
盛哉正統乙丑春歲當大比天下
貢士之来試者雲會于京至期禮
部以請
===
皇上命尚書臣濙侍郎臣英為知貢舉
官學士臣習禮侍講學士臣愉為
考試官侍讀臣嘉言編脩〔臣璉臣淵〕
〔臣世隆〕給事中臣潤教授〔臣惟勉〕教諭
〔臣敏臣諮〕為同考試官監察御史〔臣本臣誠〕
為監試官執事諸官又選朝臣之
廉慎者特賜宴以遣之入院莫不

列庶位，盡瘁事國，仰副聖心求賢輔治之誠。是盖有虞黎獻共臣之日，成周多士濟濟之時，猗歟盛哉！

正統乙丑春，歲當大比，天下貢士之来試者雲會于京。至期，禮部以請。皇上命尚書臣濙、侍郎臣英為知貢舉官，學士臣習禮、侍講學士臣愉為考試官，侍讀臣嘉言、編脩〔臣璉、臣淵、臣世隆〕、給事中臣潤、教授〔臣惟勉〕、教諭〔臣敏、臣諮〕為同考試官，監察御史〔臣本、臣誠〕為監試官。執事諸官，又選朝臣之廉慎者，特賜宴以遣之。入院，莫不
translation_en:
…be arrayed in the various official positions, exhausting their strength in service to the dynasty so as to live up to the sincerity of the Sacred Mind in seeking worthies to assist in governance. This is truly an era like that of the Lord of Yu, when the eminent men among the black-haired people all served as subjects, and a time like that of the accomplished Zhou, when the many scholars were so numerous and dignified. Oh, how magnificent!

In the spring of the yichou year of the Zhengtong reign (1445), the year of the great triennial examination, the tribute scholars from across the realm coming to be examined gathered like clouds in the capital. When the appointed time arrived, the Ministry of Rites petitioned the throne. His Majesty the Emperor commanded the Minister, Your Servant [Hu] Ying 胡濙, and the Vice Minister, Your Servant [Wang] Ying 王英, to serve as Examination Administrators; the Academician, Your Servant [Qian] Xili 錢習禮, and the Academician Expositor-in-waiting, Your Servant [Ma] Yu 馬愉, to serve as Examiners; the Reader-in-waiting, Your Servant [Miao] Jiayan 苗嘉言, the Historiographers [Your Servants Lian 璉, Yuan 淵, and Shilong 世隆], the Supervising Secretary, Your Servant Run 潤, the Instructor [Your Servant Weimian 惟勉], and the Assistant Instructors [Your Servants Min 敏 and Zi 諮] to serve as Associate Examiners; and the Investigating Censors [Your Servants Ben 本 and Cheng 誠] to serve as Examination Supervisors. As for the various administrative officers, upright and prudent court officials were also selected. A banquet was specially bestowed upon them before sending them forth. Upon entering the examination compound, there was none who did not…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
寅畏服勤乃事凡三試之得士一百
有五十人以其氏名及其文之足
為程度者書于小錄以進俾臣習禮
序之夫士之通經博古者孰不欲
擢科取仕榮其身以顯聞於人然
或不偶于時終不得名薦書者歴
代有之今爾多士際
===
盛平之世値
聖明之主以其所業捷于主司揚于
大廷策名高第致有祿仕行當歴職
中外攄其所蘊見於所施惟夙夜
匪懈思被
朝廷儲養之
恩俛竭忠藎慎乃職位砥乃名節建

盛平之世值
聖明之主以其所業捷于主司揚于
大廷策名高第致有祿仕行當歷職
中外攄其所蘊見於所施惟夙夜

朝廷儲養之
恩僶竭忠藎慎乃職位砥乃名節□
punctuated:
寅畏，服勤乃事。凡三試之，得士一百有五十人。以其氏名及其文之足為程度者書于小錄以進，俾臣習禮序之。

夫士之通經博古者，孰不欲擢科取仕，榮其身以顯聞於人？然或不偶于時，終不得名薦書者，歴代有之。今爾多士，際盛平之世，値聖明之主，以其所業捷于主司，揚于大廷，策名高第，致有祿仕。行當歴職中外，攄其所蘊，見於所施。惟夙夜匪懈，思被朝廷儲養之恩，俛竭忠藎，慎乃職位，砥乃名節，建
translation_en:
…reverent awe, diligently attending to their duties. In all, through three sessions of examination, one hundred and fifty scholars were selected. Their names and their essays worthy of serving as model answers have been inscribed in a small record for presentation to the throne, and Your Servant [Qian] Xili 錢習禮 was commanded to write a preface for it.

Now, among scholars who thoroughly understand the Classics and are broadly learned in antiquity, who does not wish to pass the examinations and obtain official appointment, bringing glory to himself and making his name illustrious among men? Yet in every dynasty there have been those who, failing to meet with an opportune time, to the end never had their names entered on the list of recommendations. Now all you scholars have encountered an era of flourishing peace and met with a sagely and enlightened ruler. Through what you have studied, you have triumphed before the examiners and will be presented at the great court, inscribing your names in the high ranks and attaining salaried office. Soon you will successively hold posts at court and in the provinces, unfolding what you have stored within and manifesting it in your administrative measures. Only be unremitting day and night, mindful of the grace of the court in nurturing and supporting you; bow your heads and exhaust your loyal devotion, be circumspect in your offices, sharpen your integrity and honor, and establish…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
立勛庸宣布惠澤上有以報稱於
國下有以利安於民則不徒榮遇於
一時百世之下人皆企慕之不能
已庶有以增科目之重其相與勉
之
翰林院學士奉政大夫錢習禮謹序
alt_text:
立勛庸宣布恵澤上有以報稱於
國下有以利安於民則不徒榮遇於
一時百世之下人皆企慕之不能
已庶有以增科目之重其相與勉
之
翰林院學士奉政大夫錢〔習禮〕謹序
punctuated:
立勛庸，宣布惠澤，上有以報稱於國，下有以利安於民，則不徒榮遇於一時，百世之下，人皆企慕之不能已，庶有以增科目之重。其相與勉之！

翰林院學士奉政大夫錢習禮謹序。
translation_en:
…establish meritorious service, and proclaim benevolent grace. Above, you will have the means to repay and prove worthy of the state; below, you will have the means to benefit and bring peace to the people. Thus, you will not merely enjoy glorious favor for a single era, but for a hundred generations to come, people will all look up to and admire you endlessly, and this may perhaps add weight to the examination system. Let everyone encourage one another in this!

Respectfully prefaced by Qian Xili 錢習禮, Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Governance.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Tenth Year of the Zhengtong Reign (1445)

Administrators of the Tribute Examination (知貢舉官):
Hu Ying 胡濙, Grand Master for Assisting toward Virtue, Rectifier of Governance and Senior Chief Minister, and Minister of Rites. (Courtesy name Yuanjie 源潔; a native of Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the gengchen year [1400].)
Wang Ying 王英, Grand Master for Proper Consultation, Director of Governance, Left Vice Minister of Rites, and concurrently Academician Expositor-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy. (Courtesy name Shiyan 時彥; a native of Jinxi County, Fuzhou Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the jiashen year [1404].)

Examiners (考試官):
Qian Xili 錢習禮, Academician of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Governance. (A native of Jishui County, Ji'an Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the xinmao year [1411].)
Ma Yu 馬愉, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Uprightness. (Courtesy name Xinghe 性和; a native of Linqu County, Qingzhou Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year [1427].)

Associate Examiners (同考試官):
Xi Jiayan 習嘉言, Reader-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Fostering Uprightness. (A native of Xinyu County, Linjiang Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the wuxu year [1418].)
Xie Lian 謝璉, Junior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Fostering Literature. (Courtesy name Zhongqi 重器; a native of Longxi County, Zhangzhou Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year [1427].)
Jiang Yuan 江淵, Junior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Fostering Literature. (Courtesy name Shiyong 時用; a native of Jiangjin County, Chongqing Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the gengxu year [1430].)
Lai Shilong 賴世隆, Junior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Fostering Literature. (Courtesy name Deshou 德受; a native of Qingliu County, Tingzhou Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the gengxu year [1430].)
Hou Run 侯潤, Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Rites. (A native of Linhai County, Taizhou Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the guichou year [1433].)
Liu Weimian 劉惟勉, Instructor in the Confucian School of Shaowu Prefecture, Fujian. (A native of Cixi County, Ningbo Prefecture; a tribute scholar [provincial graduate] of the bingwu year [1426].)
Yan Min 嚴敏, Instructor in the Confucian School of Wendeng County, Dengzhou Prefecture, Shandong. (Courtesy name Bolu 伯魯; a native of Qiantang County, Hangzhou Prefecture; a tribute scholar [provincial graduate] of the renzi year [1432].)
Dong Mi 董謐, Instructor in the Confucian School of Neihuang County, Daming Prefecture, in the Metropolitan Area (Zhili). (Courtesy name Kehui 克譓; a native of Shouguang County, Qingzhou Prefecture; a tribute scholar [provincial graduate] of the dingyou year [1417].)

Monitoring Examiners (監試官):
Yu Ben 俞本, Gentleman for Fostering Literature and Investigating Censor of the Jiangxi Circuit. (Courtesy name Lichu 立初; a native of Huating County, Songjiang Prefecture; a metropolitan graduate of the jiachen year [1424].)

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
第一場
四書
有斐君子終不可諠兮者道盛德至善民之不
能忘也
德為聖人尊為天子富有四海之內宗廟饗之
子孫保之故大德必得其位必得其祿必
得其名必得其壽
伯夷聖之清者也伊尹聖之任者也柳下惠
聖之和者也孔子聖之時者也孔子之
===
謂集大成集大成也者金聲而玉振之也
易
臨剛浸而長說而順剛中而應大亨以正天之
道也
剛健篤實輝光日新其德剛上而尚賢能止健
大正也
天地相遇品物咸章也剛遇中正天下大行也
姤之時義大矣哉
說萬物者莫說乎澤潤萬物者莫潤乎水終萬

能忘也

===
易
臨剛浸而長説而順剛中而應大亨以正天之
道也
剛健篤實輝光日新其德剛上而尚賢能止健
大正也
天地相遇品物咸章也剛遇中正天下大行也
姤之時義大矣哉
説萬物者莫説乎澤潤萬物者莫潤乎水終萬
punctuated:
第一場

四書
「有斐君子，終不可諠兮」者，道盛德至善，民之不能忘也。
德為聖人，尊為天子，富有四海之內，宗廟饗之，子孫保之。故大德必得其位，必得其祿，必得其名，必得其壽。
伯夷，聖之清者也；伊尹，聖之任者也；柳下惠，聖之和者也；孔子，聖之時者也。孔子之謂集大成。集大成也者，金聲而玉振之也。

易
臨，剛浸而長，說而順，剛中而應，大亨以正，天之道也。
剛健篤實輝光，日新其德，剛上而尚賢，能止健，大正也。
天地相遇，品物咸章也。剛遇中正，天下大行也。姤之時義大矣哉！
說萬物者莫說乎澤，潤萬物者莫潤乎水，終萬
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

"'There is the accomplished and elegant noble man; never can he be forgotten!' This expresses that because his abundant virtue and supreme goodness reached the utmost, the people are unable to forget him." [Great Learning (Daxue)]

"His virtue was that of a sage; his dignity was that of the Son of Heaven; his wealth was all within the Four Seas. He offered sacrifices in his ancestral temple, and his descendants preserved it. Therefore, one of great virtue is sure to attain his position, is sure to attain his emolument, is sure to attain his fame, and is sure to attain his longevity." [Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong)]

"Bo Yi 伯夷 was the sage who was pure; Yi Yin 伊尹 was the sage who took responsibility; Liuxia Hui 柳下惠 was the sage who was harmonious; Confucius (Kongzi 孔子) was the sage who was timely. Confucius may be called one who gathered a complete concert. Gathering a complete concert is to begin with the sound of metal bells and conclude with the resonance of jade chimes." [Mencius (Mengzi)]

Classic of Changes (Yi)

"Approach (Lin 臨): the firm advances and grows; joyous and compliant, the firm is central and finds response. Great success through correctness: this is the Way of Heaven."

"Firm, strong,笃實 [solid and substantial], and brilliantly glorious, daily renewing his virtue; the firm ascends above and honors the worthy; able to restrain strength: this is great correctness." [Great Accumulation (Dachu 大畜)]

"When heaven and earth meet, the myriad things are all manifestly displayed. When the firm meets with centrality and correctness, the Way prevails greatly throughout the world. Great indeed is the timely significance of Encounter (Gou 姤)!"

任官惟賢才，左右惟其人。臣為上為德，為下為民，其難其慎，惟和惟一。德無常師，主善為師；善無常主，協于克一。

translation_en:
…things to completion and bringing the myriad things to a new beginning, nothing is more flourishing than the Mountain (Gen).

The Book of Documents (Shu):
"In appointing to office, employ only the worthy and talented; for your close attendants, choose only the right men. A minister, in relation to his sovereign above, promotes virtue, and in relation to the people below, cares for their welfare. How difficult it is! How cautious he must be! There must be harmony; there must be unity. Virtue has no constant teacher, other than taking goodness as its teacher; goodness has no constant master, other than according with the ability to maintain unity."
"When men do not lightly esteem things, their things are an expression of virtue."
"The noble man makes taking no ease his abiding place. When he first understands the hardships of sowing and reaping and only then takes ease, he understands what the common people depend upon."
"Neither too hard nor too soft, his virtue is truly cultivated."

The Book of Odes (Shi):
"Carefully adjusted are the rabbit nets; clanging go the blows on their pegs. Stalwart is the martial warrior, shield and wall to his duke or marquis. Carefully adjusted are the rabbit nets, set at the crossroads. Stalwart is the martial warrior, a fine mate to his duke or marquis. Carefully adjusted are the rabbit nets, set in the midst of the forest. Stalwart is the martial warrior, heart and confidant to his duke or marquis."
"The Feng waters flowed eastward, through the achievement of Yu. Where the four quarters converged, the august king was ruler. Splendid indeed was the august king! In the capital of Hao with its Circular Moat, from the west and from the east, from the south and from the north, there were none who did not think of submitting. Splendid indeed was the august king!"
"What is the announcement thereof? The bamboo and wooden vessels are clean and fine. The friends assisting at the sacrifice assist with dignified demeanor. Their dignified demeanor is most timely, and the noble lord has filial sons. Of filial sons there will be no lack; forever will blessings be bestowed upon your kind."

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
感鬼神化強暴致物類之應者以孰為著德
施於人至於享祿位膺壽考延子孫之慶者
以孰為最其明言之毋泛舉以對
問湯誥曰惟皇上帝降衷于下民若有恒性子
思作中庸曰天命之謂性曰降衷曰天命何
所分歟孔子曰繼之者善成之者性孟子則
言性善孔孟所言善性性善同歟異歟至若
荀揚韓之論性其說異矣近世儒者亦有謂
性未有善惡又有謂性無善惡又云謂之善
===
者只是贊嘆之辭其說然歟否歟抑何所折
衷歟人稟陰陽五行之理氣而生宜均善而
無惡也何以有剛柔暴險智愚之不同歟五
常之謂性孟子止言四端朱子亦曰與之以
仁義禮智之性皆不及信何歟性發而為情
中庸不曰性情而曰中和何歟中庸之言情
四程子乃曰其中動而七情出焉又何歟七情
於五性果何所本歟請明辨之
問道原於天地而貫乎古今人之所當共由而

感鬼神、化強暴、致物類之應者，以孰為著？德施於人，至於享祿位、膺壽考、延子孫之慶者，以孰為最？其明言之，毋泛舉以對。

問：《湯誥》曰：「惟皇上帝，降衷于下民，若有恒性。」子思作《中庸》曰：「天命之謂性。」曰「降衷」、曰「天命」，何所分歟？孔子曰：「繼之者善，成之者性。」孟子則言「性善」。孔、孟所言「善性」、「性善」，同歟？異歟？至若荀、揚、韓之論性，其說異矣。近世儒者，亦有謂性未有善惡，又有謂性無善惡，又云謂之善者只是贊嘆之辭。其說然歟？否歟？抑何所折衷歟？人稟陰陽五行之理氣而生，宜均善而無惡也，何以有剛柔、暴險、智愚之不同歟？五常之謂性，孟子止言四端，朱子亦曰「與之以仁義禮智之性」，皆不及信，何歟？性發而為情，《中庸》不曰「性情」而曰「中和」，何歟？《中庸》之言情四，程子乃曰「其中動而七情出焉」，又何歟？七情於五性，果何所本歟？請明辨之。

問：道原於天地而貫乎古今，人之所當共由而
translation_en:
… move ghosts and spirits, transform the violent and cruel, and elicit auspicious responses from creatures and things, who is the most notable? And as for bestowing virtue upon others to the point of enjoying official emoluments and rank, receiving long life, and extending blessings to one's descendants, who is the foremost? State it clearly, and do not reply with vague generalities.

Question: The "Announcement of Tang" (Tang gao) says: "The august High God has conferred an unbiased moral sense upon the people below; compliance with it constitutes their constant nature." When Zisi composed the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), he said: "What Heaven imparts is called nature." Between speaking of "conferring an unbiased moral sense" and "what Heaven imparts," what is the distinction? Confucius said: "That which continues it is goodness; that which completes it is nature." Mencius, for his part, spoke of "human nature being good." What Confucius and Mencius spoke of—goodness and nature, and nature being good—are they the same or different? As for the discussions of human nature by Xunzi, Yang Xiong, and Han Yu, their doctrines differed. Among scholars of recent ages, there have also been those who say that human nature does not yet have good or evil, others who say that human nature has neither good nor evil, and further say that calling it "good" is merely an expression of praise and admiration. Are these doctrines right or wrong? Or how should they be adjudicated? Human beings are born endowed with the principle (li) and vital force (qi) of yin, yang, and the Five Phases, so they ought to be uniformly good and without evil; why then are there differences of firm and yielding, violent and treacherous, wise and foolish? The Five Constant Virtues are called human nature, yet Mencius spoke only of the Four Beginnings, and Master Zhu [Zhu Xi] likewise said "endowing them with a nature of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom"—neither of them mentioning trustworthiness (xin); why is this? When nature is aroused, it becomes the feelings (qing); why does the Doctrine of the Mean not speak of "nature and feelings" but instead speaks of "equilibrium and harmony" (zhong he)? The Doctrine of the Mean mentions four feelings, whereas Master Cheng [Cheng Yi] said, "When the center is stirred, the seven feelings issue forth"—why is this so as well? Upon what, indeed, are the seven feelings grounded in relation to the five virtues of human nature? Please distinguish these matters clearly.

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
不可須臾離者見之於易已有天地人之道
何子思謂誠者天之道誠之者人之道而不
及地之道何歟先儒於中庸自二十一章以
下分天道人道而言其旨可得詳歟夫子於
顏淵問仁告以克己復禮仲弓問仁告以主
敬行恕先儒釋以乾道坤道而不及人之道
又何歟有所謂聖人之道君子之道果何所
分歟堯舜夫子皆聖人道固同也而孟子曰
堯舜之道孝弟而已矣曾子曰夫子之道忠
===
恕而已矣何其道之不同歟夫子又謂孝弟
為仁之次中庸謂忠恕違道不遠何歟其詳
析而明言之
問教民以學校為先而風俗繫焉三代學制教
法與其風化之盛可得聞歟漢興未遑學校
孝文時蜀守興學止於一郡而已而論者曰
漢自高惠至於文景黎民醇厚幾致刑措然
則風俗之美果何道以致之歟武帝始立太
學及郡國學行之有其實歟光武起太學明

punctuated:
不可須臾離者。見之於《易》，已有天地人之道，何子思謂「誠者，天之道；誠之者，人之道」，而不及地之道，何歟？先儒於《中庸》自二十一章以下，分天道、人道而言，其旨可得詳歟？夫子於顏淵問仁，告以「克己復禮」；仲弓問仁，告以「主敬行恕」。先儒釋以乾道、坤道，而不及人之道，又何歟？有所謂聖人之道、君子之道，果何所分歟？堯、舜、夫子皆聖人，道固同也。而孟子曰：「堯舜之道，孝弟而已矣。」曾子曰：「夫子之道，忠恕而已矣。」何其道之不同歟？夫子又謂孝弟為仁之次，《中庸》謂「忠恕違道不遠」，何歟？其詳析而明言之。

問：教民以學校為先，而風俗繫焉。三代學制、教法與其風化之盛，可得聞歟？漢興，未遑學校；孝文時，蜀守興學，止於一郡而已。而論者曰，漢自高、惠至於文、景，黎民醇厚，幾致刑措。然則風俗之美，果何道以致之歟？武帝始立太學及郡國學，行之有其實歟？光武起太學，明
translation_en:
…cannot be departed from for even an instant. As seen in the Book of Changes (Yi), there are already the Ways of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity. Why, then, did Zisi say, "Sincerity is the Way of Heaven; attaining sincerity is the Way of Humanity," without mentioning the Way of Earth? When former Confucians, from chapter twenty-one of the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) onward, discussed it by distinguishing between the Way of Heaven and the Way of Humanity, can the purport of this be explained in detail? When Yan Yuan asked about humaneness (ren), the Master answered him with "overcoming the self and returning to ritual propriety"; when Zhonggong asked about humaneness, he answered him with "holding fast to reverence and practicing reciprocity." Why, again, did former Confucians explain these in terms of the Way of Qian [Heaven] and the Way of Kun [Earth], without mentioning the Way of Humanity? There are what are called the Way of the Sage and the Way of the Gentleman—how are they actually distinguished? Yao, Shun, and the Master [Confucius] were all sages, so their Way was surely the same. Yet Mencius said, "The Way of Yao and Shun is filial piety and fraternal duty, and nothing more," while Zengzi said, "The Master's Way is conscientiousness and reciprocity (zhongshu), and nothing more." Why were their Ways not the same? Moreover, the Master said that filial piety and fraternal duty are secondary [in the classification of the scholar], and the Doctrine of the Mean says that "conscientiousness and reciprocity are not far from the Way"—why is this? Analyze these matters in detail and state your answer clearly.

Question: In instructing the people, schools come first, and customs and mores depend upon them. May we hear about the school systems and methods of instruction of the Three Dynasties, along with the flourishing of their moral transformation? When the Han arose, it did not yet have leisure to establish schools; during the reign of Emperor Xiaowen, the Governor of Shu promoted schools, but this was limited to a single commandery. Yet commentators say that in the Han, from Emperors Gao and Hui down to Wen and Jing, the common people were simple and honest, and punishments were almost set aside entirely. If so, by what means was the excellence of their customs actually brought about? Emperor Wu first established the Imperial University (Taixue) as well as schools in the commanderies and principalities—was there real substance in how this was carried out? Emperor Guangwu rebuilt the Imperial University, and Emperor Ming…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
帝幸辟雍其實可舉歟當時郡國之學亦舉
行歟又有四姓小侯學為誰立歟兩漢風俗
所尚亦有可論歟唐太宗增學舎廣生員又
設六學皆隸國子監生徒各有數可考其詳
歟當時風化有可取歟宋初開國子監州縣
學未立儒者依山林間講授而四書院為尤
著州縣之學立於何年起於何人所言歟宋
之風化亦有可言歟請詳陳之毋泛毋畧
問三代人才之盛不可尚矣漢唐宋之興士之
===
出為世用者建政立事尊主庇民顯于當時
傳之後世者不可以一二遽數姑畧舉而言
之輔成君業俾之敬而不敢慢可正君心引
之志於仁而不忘正直足以懾阿諛忠厚足
以闢忍刻所立事業竒偉而專以四者為之
本忠亮居位以匡其君諳練在朝不恤其身
憂國家才氣老成以振作士類為己任安危
疑德業盛大足追配古人而無愧至於能受
人言雖忤之而不慍是數子者皆先儒之所

punctuated:
帝幸辟雍，其實可舉歟？當時郡國之學亦舉行歟？又有四姓小侯學，為誰立歟？兩漢風俗所尚，亦有可論歟？唐太宗增學舎、廣生員，又設六學，皆隸國子監，生徒各有數，可考其詳歟？當時風化有可取歟？宋初開國子監，州縣學未立，儒者依山林間講授，而四書院為尤著。州縣之學立於何年？起於何人所言歟？宋之風化亦有可言歟？請詳陳之，毋泛毋畧。
問：三代人才之盛，不可尚矣。漢、唐、宋之興，士之出為世用者，建政立事、尊主庇民，顯于當時、傳之後世者，不可以一二遽數。姑畧舉而言之：輔成君業，俾之敬而不敢慢，可正君心，引之志於仁而不忘；正直足以懾阿諛，忠厚足以闢忍刻；所立事業竒偉，而專以四者為之本；忠亮居位以匡其君，諳練在朝不恤其身；憂國家，才氣老成，以振作士類為己任；安危疑，德業盛大，足追配古人而無愧；至於能受人言，雖忤之而不慍。是數子者，皆先儒之所
translation_en:
… Emperor Ming visited the Imperial College (Biyong)—can the concrete facts of these be cited? Were the schools of the commanderies and principalities also operating at that time? Furthermore, there was the School for Junior Marquises of the Four Surnames—for whom was it established? Can what was valued in the customs of the Western and Eastern Han also be discussed? Emperor Taizong of the Tang expanded the school buildings, increased the number of students, and established the Six Schools, all subordinate to the Directorate of Education (Guozijian), each having a set quota of students—can the details of this be examined? Was there anything commendable in the moral transformation of that era? At the beginning of the Song, the Directorate of Education was opened, while prefectural and county schools were not yet established; Confucian scholars taught in retreats among the mountains and forests, and the Four Academies were especially renowned. In what year were the prefectural and county schools established, and from whose proposal did they originate? Is there also something to be said about the moral transformation of the Song? Please set this forth in detail, being neither vague nor cursory.

Question: The flourishing of men of talent in the Three Dynasties cannot be surpassed. With the rise of the Han, Tang, and Song, scholars who came forth to be of service to the world—establishing governance and accomplishing deeds, honoring the ruler and protecting the people, distinguished in their own times and remembered by later generations—cannot be quickly counted one or two at a time. Let us provisionally mention a few in outline: one who assisted in fulfilling his ruler's enterprise, making him reverent so that he dared not be negligent, and was able to rectify the ruler's mind, guiding him to set his will on benevolence without forgetting; one whose uprightness sufficed to overawe flatterers and whose loyal generosity sufficed to repel cruelty and harshness; one whose accomplishments were extraordinary and great, yet who exclusively took four things as his foundation; one who occupied office with loyal integrity to rectify his ruler, and who was experienced at court without regard for his own person; one who worried over the state, mature in talent and spirit, taking the rousing and encouragement of the literati as his personal responsibility; one who stabilized the state amid peril and doubt, whose virtuous achievements were so grand and great as to match the ancients without shame; and one who went so far as to be able to accept the words of others, not growing angry even when opposed. These several gentlemen were all those whom former Confucians…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
四書
德為聖人尊為天子富有四海之內宗廟饗之子
孫保之故大德必得其位必得其禄必得其名
必得其壽
同考試官編脩謝批此篇善形容大孝之實異
於眾作故表而出之
考試官侍講學士馬批議論有據詞簡理明可取
考試官學士錢批析理明遣詞順可取
===
惟孝之在於聖人者有其實故福之集於聖人者有
可必盖孝者得福之本聖人之孝天下莫能加則諸
福之至自有不期然而然者矣今夫世之人欲孝其
親者多矣而舜則謂之大孝果何由而見之人孰不
欲其子之賢舜則濬哲而文明温恭而允塞德為聖
人焉居五位之尊至貴而無倫而親為天子父是尊
之至也有四海之廣至富而無敵而以天下養其親
是養之至也欲其奉先也禘黄帝而郊嚳祖顓頊而
宗堯祭有以盡其誠而宗廟饗之矣欲其遺後也虞

"In virtue he was a sage; in honor he was the Son of Heaven; in wealth he possessed all within the four seas. It was his ancestral temple that received the sacrifices, and it was his descendants who preserved the sacrifices to him. Therefore, he who possesses great virtue will certainly attain his position, will certainly attain his emolument, will certainly attain his fame, and will certainly attain his longevity."

Because the filial piety residing in a sage possesses true substance, the blessings that gather upon a sage can be counted on with certainty. For filial piety is the root of obtaining blessings; when a sage's filial piety is such that nothing in the world can surpass it, the arrival of all blessings naturally comes about without being sought. Now, there are many people in the world who wish to be filial to their parents, yet Shun was called a man of great filial piety—how indeed can this be seen? Who does not wish for his son to be worthy? Shun was profound, wise, and accomplished, gentle, reverent, and sincerely upright; in virtue he was a sage. Occupying the venerable fifth-line position [of the ruler], utterly noble and without peer, so that his father became the father of the Son of Heaven—this is the utmost of honor. 思封於夏，胡公封於周，慶有以延於世而子孫保之矣。然孝者，德之實行。聖人之孝既有其實，則德之大從可知矣。故雖無心於得福，而天之福聖人者，自不容他適矣。以堯揖遜而受禪，此大德必得其位也；禹任土方以作貢，此大德必得其祿也；以及為法於天下、可傳於後世之名，百有十歲之壽，何莫非大德而必得之乎？故曰：惟孝之在於聖人者有其實，故福之集於聖人者有可必者，此也。抑考《中庸》此章以其費之大者而言，故引孔子稱大舜之事以明之。蓋由庸行之常推之以至其極，以見斯道之用為甚廣也；而其所以然者，則其體為甚微矣。故曰：「君子之道費而隱。」學者不可以不知。

… [Yu] Si 虞思 was enfeoffed under the Xia, and Duke Hu 胡公 was enfeoffed under the Zhou; thus his blessings were extended through the generations, and his descendants preserved them. Now filial piety is the substantive practice of virtue. Since the filial piety of the sage possessed such substance, the greatness of his virtue can accordingly be known. Therefore, even though he had no intention of obtaining blessings, the blessings that Heaven bestowed upon the sage naturally could not go elsewhere. Receiving the abdication from Yao 堯 through deferential yielding—this was great virtue necessarily obtaining its position; Yu 禹 assessing the lands of the regions to institute tribute—this was great virtue necessarily obtaining its emolument; and reaching as far as a fame that served as a model for the world and could be transmitted to later generations, and a longevity of one hundred and ten years—which of these was not necessarily obtained through great virtue? Therefore it is said: It is precisely because the filial piety residing in the sage possessed substance that the blessings gathering upon the sage could be counted on with certainty. Moreover, if we examine this chapter of the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong 中庸), it speaks in terms of the greatness of the Way's広far-reaching manifestations; hence it cites Confucius's praise of the affairs of Great Shun 舜 to elucidate it. For it extends from the constancy of ordinary actions to their utmost limit in order to show that the function of this Way is exceedingly broad, while the reason why it is so is that its substance is exceedingly subtle. Therefore it is said: "The Way of the noble man is far-reaching and yet hidden." Scholars must not fail to know this.

"Bo Yi 伯夷 was the pure one among the sages; Yi Yin 伊尹 was the responsible one among the sages; Liuxia Hui 柳下惠 was the harmonious one among the sages; Confucius was the timely one among the sages. In Confucius we have what is called a 'complete concert' (ji dacheng 集大成). A 'complete concert' is when the metallic sound of the bells is given, and the jadestone chimes conclude it."
Li Yongxiu 李庸脩

有一偏之聖，有全體之聖，故大賢既分言於前，而復取喻於後也。盖三子之行，各極於一偏，猶作樂而備一音之小成；夫子兼三子而為全體之聖，豈不猶集眾樂之小成而為一大成也哉？今夫人固有志於清者，未能不出於思勉；惟伯夷之志，無所雜而為清之極，非聖之清乎？人固有志於任者，未能不拘於去就；惟伊尹之心，則以天下為已任，而所任者重，非聖之任乎？至於和而失之流者，人情之常；惟栁下惠之行，則無所異而為聖之和也。然三子之行，清者偏於清而不能任，任者偏於任而不能和，猶春夏秋冬之各一其時。若吾夫子，則無可無不可，盖兼三子之所以聖者而時出之，則猶太和元氣之流行於四時也，非為聖之時乎？夫既為聖之時，則不拘於夷之清，而兼乎尹之任矣；不拘於尹之任，而全乎惠之和矣。若此，不謂之集大成可乎？然既謂之集大成，得不即音樂以明之乎？夫樂之作也，八音並奏，於其未作而先擊鎛

There is sagehood of a single aspect, and there is sagehood of the whole substance; therefore, the great worthy [Mencius] first speaks of them separately and then draws a metaphor afterward. Indeed, the conduct of the three masters each reached the ultimate in one aspect, just like performing music and completing the minor accomplishment of a single instrument's sound; the Master [Confucius] combined the three masters to become a sage of the whole substance—is this not like gathering the minor accomplishments of various musical instruments to form one great concert? Now, while there are certainly people who set their minds on purity, they cannot help doing so out of deliberation and effort; only the will of Boyi 伯夷 was free of all admixture and reached the ultimate of purity—was he not the sage of purity? While there are certainly people who set their minds on taking responsibility, they cannot help being bound by considerations of leaving or taking office; only the heart of Yi Yin 伊尹 took the whole world as his personal responsibility, and what he bore was heavy—was he not the sage of responsibility? As for being harmonious yet erring by drifting with the current, that is the common way of human feelings; only the conduct of Liuxia Hui 柳下惠 made no ostentatious distinctions and thus was the sage of harmony. Yet in the conduct of the three masters, the pure one leaned toward purity and could not take on responsibility, while the responsible one leaned toward responsibility and could not be harmonious, just like spring, summer, autumn, and winter each having its single season. As for our Master, he had nothing that he must or must not do; indeed, he combined that whereby the three masters were sages and brought it forth according to the time, just like the primordial vital energy of supreme harmony circulating through all four seasons—was he not the sage of timeliness? Since he was the sage of timeliness, he was not bound by Boyi's purity, yet encompassed Yi Yin's responsibility; he was not bound by Yi Yin's responsibility, yet perfected Liuxia Hui's harmony. Being such as this, how could one not call it "gathering the great concert"? Yet since it is called "gathering the great concert," how could one not turn directly to music to illustrate it? … bell to proclaim its sound, and waits until it has concluded before striking the single chime-stone to gather in its resonance. Proclaiming to begin it, and gathering in to end it—between the two, the threads run through coherently with nothing left incomplete; this is combining the small completions of the various sounds to form one great completion. When the discussion reaches this point, one knows how our Master's sagehood could ever be spoken of on the same day as the three worthies! Examining further the text below, where it says, "Beginning an orderly progression is the work of wisdom; ending an orderly progression is the work of sagehood," this further clarifies the ultimate perfection of the Sage's wisdom and sagehood. And where it says, "Wisdom may be compared to skill, and sagehood may be compared to strength; it is like shooting from beyond a hundred paces: that the arrow reaches is due to your strength, but that it hits the mark is not due to your strength," this further explains the meaning of wisdom and sagehood and shows the difference between partiality and completeness. The reader must not fail to know this.

Examiner Instructor (xuezheng) Qian comments: The diction and reasoning are concise and clear, deeply grasping the purport of this Classic.

When one understands that the virtue accumulated within oneself is exceedingly abundant, one then understands that the Way manifested in action conforms to correctness. Indeed, what is possessed within must take form without. When the superior man accumulates and stores up his virtue so that he truly possesses it within himself, then in his honoring the worthy and restraining the vigorous, where could he go and not act with correctness? When the sage explained the hexagram name and hexagram statement of Daxu ("Great Accumulation"), his meaning was profound indeed.

Now, in the hexagram Daxu, the inner trigram is Qian, and the virtue of Qian is firm and vigorous; the outer trigram is Gen, and the virtue of Gen is earnest and substantial. As for being firm and vigorous: being firm means not [yielding?], and being vigorous means being ceaseless. As for being earnest and substantial: being earnest means being generously thick, and being substantial means being full and real. Because he is earnest and substantial […], harmony and compliance accumulate within while glorious splendor shines forth without—this is what is meant by "when there is fullness and substance along with brilliance, [it is called greatness?]." And because he is firm and vigorous, what is attained within himself is enduring and ceaseless—this is what is meant by "[daily renewal?] is called abundant virtue." Is this not what is meant by the virtue accumulated within oneself being exceedingly abundant?

[Since one's?] virtue is already abundant, it is sufficient to serve as the foundation for nourishing the worthy; yet if the worthy are not nourished by us, how can the efficacy of accumulating virtue be seen? Therefore, the yang firmness of the Nine originally resided in the fifth place, and now advances to reside at the top; thus the ruler of the Six in the fifth place honors and exalts him—this is the meaning of "exalting the worthy." Gen represents stopping and is above; Qian represents vigor and dwells below; thus, with the correctness of a single firm line, it restrains the advance of the utmost vigor—this is the meaning of "restraining the vigorous." Because one exalts the worthy, one will surely dismiss slanderers, keep beauties at a distance, despise wealth, and esteem virtue—without great correctness, one could not do so. Because one restrains the vigorous, one will surely be resolute and unyielding, capable of overcoming external things—this too can only be done through great correctness. Is this not what is meant by the Way manifested in action conforming to correctness?

translation_en:
… "Heaven within the mountain: Great Accumulation (Daxu). The noble man thus acquaints himself with many words of antiquity and deeds of the past, in order to accumulate his virtue." This further illustrates that if a person wishes to accumulate his virtue, he must rely on the effort of learning and inquiry to achieve its greatness. In this way, proceeding from firm strength and substantial sincerity to daily renewal, virtue comes to be possessed within oneself; and only thereafter can one honor the worthy and restrain the strong. The meaning is that there must first be a great inner store before there can be great outward implementation. Ah, how supreme!

"For gladdening the myriad things, nothing is more gladdening than the marsh; for moistening the myriad things, nothing is more moistening than water; for bringing the myriad things to an end and bringing the myriad things to a beginning, nothing is more flourishing than Gen (Keeping Still)."
Xu Xuan 徐瑄
Comment by Associate Examiner Compiler Xie 謝: This topic is based on King Wen's Later Heaven Sequence of the Classic of Changes (Yi) and speaks of the functions of the sixderived trigrams ("six children"). Among the various essays, few were able to elucidate its meaning. This piece demonstrates a clear personal grasp and deeply captures the sage's intent in explaining the trigrams.
Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Ma 馬: Able to elucidate the purport of the "Explanation of the Trigrams" (Shuogua); he must be thoroughly versed in the Classic and deserves to be placed among the selected.
Comment by Examiner Academician Qian 錢: His comprehension is unerring and his elucidation penetrating—a fine piece of work.

As for how the creative and transformative forces bring things to completion and serve as their end and beginning, one must set forth in order the functions of the trigram images. Indeed, the completion of things certainly relies upon the work of moistening and gladdening; yet as for that whereby they are brought to a completed end and a new beginning, must it not be rooted in the work of Gen, stopping? Justly did the sage who explained the trigrams have reason to set forth their functions in sequence! Moreover, filling heaven and earth, teeming in such varied multitudes—these are the myriad things…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
也形形色色若此其不齊者亦萬物也方其齊乎巽
也但撓之以風而潤說之功未著相見乎離也但熯
之以火而成物之功未見其所以和說而成其物者
得不在於澤乎蓋澤者兌之象也在四方則居西於
四時則為秋萬物於斯時也則和說以成其質收斂
以遂其性非兌澤之功乎故曰說萬物者莫說乎澤
也物既說矣其所以滋潤而固其物者得不在於水
乎蓋水為坎之象居乎正北於時為冬萬物於斯時
也翕然以滋養寂然以貞固非坎水之功乎故曰潤
===
萬物者莫潤乎水也至若艮之為卦位乎東北之方
當乎冬春之交然為物之終者其用在乎坎若無與
於艮也而所以成其終者必在於艮焉為物之始者
其用在乎震亦若無與於艮也而所以成其始者必
在於艮焉又非終萬物始萬物者莫盛於艮乎抑考
此章說卦聖人序六子之用而潤說終始皆所以成
乎物也然而潤說之義皆以象言而終始者獨以卦
言何也蓋潤說者以其象而終始萬物者其義有不
係於象也學者詳之

punctuated: 也；形形色色若此其不齊者，亦萬物也。方其齊乎巽也，但撓之以風，而潤說之功未著；相見乎離也，但熯之以火，而成物之功未見。其所以和說而成其物者，得不在於澤乎？蓋澤者，兌之象也。在四方則居西，於四時則為秋。萬物於斯時也，則和說以成其質，收斂以遂其性，非兌澤之功乎？故曰：「說萬物者，莫說乎澤也。」物既說矣，其所以滋潤而固其物者，得不在於水乎？蓋水為坎之象，居乎正北，於時為冬。萬物於斯時也，翕然以滋養，寂然以貞固，非坎水之功乎？故曰：「潤萬物者，莫潤乎水也。」至若艮之為卦，位乎東北之方，當乎冬春之交。然為物之終者，其用在乎坎，若無與於艮也，而所以成其終者，必在於艮焉；為物之始者，其用在乎震，亦若無與於艮也，而所以成其始者，必在於艮焉。又非「終萬物始萬物者，莫盛於艮」乎？抑考此章，說卦聖人序六子之用，而潤、說、終、始皆所以成乎物也。然而潤、說之義皆以象言，而終、始者獨以卦言，何也？蓋潤、說者以其象，而終、始萬物者，其義有不係於象也。學者詳之。
translation_en:
… and those that take on such myriad forms and colors in all their unevenness are likewise the myriad things. Just when they are brought into alignment in Xun (Gentle/Wind), they are merely stirred by the wind, and the work of moistening and gladdening is not yet manifest; when they become mutually visible in Li (Clinging/Fire), they are merely parched by fire, and the work of bringing things to completion is not yet seen. Does not that by which things are harmonized, gladdened, and brought to completion lie in the marsh? For the marsh is the image of Dui (Joyous). Among the four directions it occupies the west, and among the four seasons it corresponds to autumn. At this time, the myriad things are harmonized and gladdened so as to complete their substance, and gathered in so as to fulfill their nature—is this not the work of the marsh of Dui? Therefore it is said: "Of all things that gladden the myriad things, none is more gladdening than the marsh."

Once things have been gladdened, does not that by which they are nourished, moistened, and made firm lie in water? For water is the image of Kan (Abysmal), occupying the due north, and in time corresponding to winter. At this time, the myriad things are drawn together to be nourished and stilled to become firm and贞 (steadfast)—is this not the work of the water of Kan? Therefore it is said: "Of all things that moisten the myriad things, none is more moistening than water."

As for the trigram Gen (Keeping Still/Mountain), it is positioned in the northeast, corresponding to the juncture between winter and spring. Now, as for bringing things to an end, that function belongs to Kan and would seem to have nothing to do with Gen, yet that by which their ending is brought to completion necessarily lies in Gen; and as for giving things their beginning, that function belongs to Zhen (Arousing/Thunder) and would likewise seem to have nothing to do with Gen, yet that by which their beginning is brought to completion necessarily lies in Gen. Is this not again why "of all things that bring the myriad things to an end and give the myriad things their beginning, none is more flourishing than Gen"?

Furthermore, if we examine this chapter, the sage who composed the "Discussion of the Trigrams" (Shuogua) set forth in sequence the functions of the six sons [the six derivative trigrams], and moistening, gladdening, ending, and beginning are all means of bringing things to completion. Yet why is it that the meanings of moistening and gladdening are both spoken of in terms of their images [water and marsh], whereas ending and beginning alone are spoken of in terms of the trigram [Gen] itself? It is because moistening and gladdening act through their physical images, whereas in bringing the myriad things to an end and to a beginning, the meaning is not bound to the physical image alone. Let scholars examine this closely.

"In appointing to office, employ only the worthy and talented; for those at your left and right, choose only the right men. A minister, in relation to his sovereign above, serves to cultivate his virtue; in relation to the people below, he serves to care for the people. How difficult it is! How cautious one must be! Seek harmony and unity. Virtue has no constant teacher; taking goodness as master makes one a teacher. Goodness has no constant master; it consists in harmonizing with the mind that has attained oneness."
By Lu Chongxian 魯崇賢
Comment by Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Yi 侇 [?]: "This essay is limpid in style and rich in principle. Free of trite imitation, it is a masterpiece."

When a great minister counsels his ruler, he not only wishes him to fulfill the Way of establishing offices and employing men, but also wishes him to grasp the essentials of learning from others in order to do good. For that upon which a minister's office bears is extremely weighty, and the cultivation of the ruler's virtue is even more difficult; therefore, not only must one seek the right men when appointing to office, but there must also be an essential principle in doing good. Fitting indeed was it that Yi Yin set these matters forth in detail to instruct Tai Jia 太甲! Yi Yin's meaning was as if to say: The empire is so vast that a ruler cannot govern it alone; he must establish a multitude of officials and envoys to govern it. All those distributed across the court and provinces are the various officials; for the various officials, one must seek those equal to their duties, and it will do only if men of virtue occupy positions of rank and men of talent hold actual offices. Those who assist and stand at the ruler's left and right are the great ministers; for the great ministers, it is even more crucial to obtain the right men, and it will do only if they combine both talent and virtue and have long enjoyed lofty prestige and reputation. text:
君民之重上焉而陳善閑邪獻可替否承弼厥辟以
成其德下焉而所欲與聚所惡勿施康濟小民以利
其生臣職所係其重如此建官之際容可輕乎必也
難於任用重之而不敢易慎於聽察謹之而不敢忽此
所以防小人使之無所售其奸可否相濟待之恊和
而無乖終始惟一信之專一而不二又所以任君子
使之得以行其道官使得人固足以為君德之助又
豈可自廣狹人而不樂取諸人以為善哉德無眾善
天下之德無一定之師惟善是從則凡有善者皆可
===
師此資諸人者善原於一天下之善無一定之主惟
一其心則其所取者無不善此反諸已者始也博而
求之於不一之善有以得一本萬殊之理終也約而
會之於至一之理有以達萬殊一本之妙此聖學始
終條理之序而人主取人為善之要也太甲至是而
得與聞焉其才固有大過人者觀太甲復辟之初伊
尹致仕而去恐其德不純一任用非人作書訓之尤
惓惓於為德為民之語實伊尹自任以天下之重上
欲堯舜其君下欲堯舜其民之心雖老而不忘太甲

translation_en:
… weighty responsibilities toward both the ruler and the people. Above, they set forth what is good and guard against perversity, proposing what is acceptable and rejecting what is objectionable, supporting and assisting their sovereign so as to perfect his virtue; below, they gather for the people what they desire and do not impose upon them what they hate, bringing peace and relief to the common folk so as to benefit their livelihoods. When that upon which a minister's office depends is as weighty as this, how could one take the establishment of offices lightly? One must be deliberate in making appointments, treating them as weighty and not daring to be casual; and one must be circumspect in listening and observing, treating them with caution and not daring to be negligent. This is the means to guard against petty men, leaving them nowhere to peddle their treachery. Balancing approval and disapproval to complement one another, one treats them with harmony and without discord; remaining consistent from beginning to end, one trusts them with single-minded devotion and without duplicity. This, in turn, is the means to employ gentlemen, enabling them to put their Way into practice.

When offices and posts obtain the right men, that is certainly sufficient to serve as an aid to the ruler's virtue; yet how could he be self-important and belittle others, rather than delighting in taking from others in order to do good? Virtue does not consist of a single goodness [alone], and for virtue in the world there is no fixed teacher; if one follows only what is good, then anyone who possesses goodness can be taken as a teacher—this is drawing upon others. Goodness originates in unity, and for goodness in the world there is no fixed master; if one unifies one's mind, then whatever one adopts will never fail to be good—this is reflecting within oneself. In the beginning, by broadly seeking it among diverse forms of goodness, one is able to grasp the principle of one root and myriad manifestations; in the end, by concisely bringing it together in the supreme unity of principle, one is able to penetrate the subtlety of myriad manifestations returning to one root. This is the orderly sequence of the beginning and end of sagely learning, and the essential way for a ruler to take from others in order to do good.

That Tai Jia 太甲 reached this point and was able to hear of these teachings shows that his talent certainly far surpassed that of ordinary men. When we observe that at the beginning of Tai Jia's restoration to the throne, as Yi Yin 伊尹 was retiring from office and departing, he feared that the king's virtue might not be pure and unified and that he might employ the wrong men, and so composed a document to instruct him—dwelling with special earnestness on words about cultivating virtue and caring for the people—this truly came from Yi Yin's taking upon himself the weighty responsibility of the world: a mind that above desired to make his ruler a Yao 堯 or a Shun 舜, and below desired to make his people the people of a Yao or a Shun, which even in old age he did not forget. "The noble man makes 'not indulging in ease' his dwelling place. Only when he first knows the hardships of sowing and reaping and thereafter takes his ease will he know what the common people depend upon."
Shang Lu 商輅
Comment by Associate Examiner Historiographer-compiler Lai: All seven essays across the entire examination are excellent. This essay elucidates "not indulging in ease" and "thereafter taking ease" in a way that sets it apart from the crowd of compositions; it ought to be singled out and published.
Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Ma: The diction is clear and fluent, and the exposition of principle is pertinent and incisive. Worthy of selection.
Comment by Examiner Academician Qian: This topic is inherently difficult to write on, yet this essay alone sets forth the Duke of Zhou's intention in admonishing his ruler with thorough, repeated elaboration, surpassing the crowd of compositions. He is a fine scholar.

A ruler ought to situate himself in diligence without ever departing from it at any time; crucially, he must abide in ease only through diligence, thereby knowing what the people rely upon. For diligence is what the Way of the ruler ought to fulfill to the utmost. If perchance he does not know the toil of farming and yet occupies the comfort of the ruler's position, how then can he know what the livelihood of the people relies upon? In antiquity, the Duke of Zhou composed a document to instruct King Cheng, saying that ease is what a ruler ought to guard against, whereas not indulging in ease is what a ruler ought to strive for. Yet he did not merely say "not indulging in ease," but further said "makes 'not indulging in ease' his dwelling place"—here "place" (suo 所) is like a dwelling place (chusuo 處所). When a ruler takes diligence as his dwelling place, then in going out and coming in, in rising and sitting, he is necessarily therein, never departing from it for an instant; in movement and stillness, in eating and resting, he is likewise therein, never diverging from it for a moment. translation_en: … is just like his brief moments, and his end is just like his beginning. Why would one act like this? Is it because he hates ease and pleasure and is fond of worry and toil? Truly it is because among the achievements that sustain the people, none is greater than sowing and reaping; and among the tasks of the four classes of people, none is more toilsome than sowing and reaping. When planting in the fields, hoeing, covering the seed, weeding, and hilling the roots, they labor amid summer heat and rain; when bringing the harvest to the threshing floor, gathering, reaping, and cutting the grain with sickles, they toil diligently among the acres. Exhausting their strength across three seasons to reap the harvest of a single year—how truly arduous is the work of agriculture! Knowing this, the ruler, though dwelling deep within the ninefold palace enclosures, dares not indulge in leisure, nor lightly rob the people of their farming seasons, lest he cause them the lament that their fields have all gone to puddles and weeds; sitting in stately repose with folded hands upon the sovereign throne, he has no leisure to rest in comfort, nor does he overtax their strength, lest he cause them the grief of having to abandon their harvesting. Thus we know that the livelihood of the people depends upon sowing and reaping just as fish depend on water and trees depend on soil. Without water, fish have no means to nourish themselves; without soil, trees cannot take root by themselves; and without sowing and reaping, the people suffer hunger and starvation with nothing on which to rely for life, wandering destitute and losing their homes. How imperative it is that he who rules All under Heaven must not fail to understand the hardships of agriculture! Rightly did the Duke of Zhou (Zhougong) begin with this when instructing King Cheng (Chengwang). Yet the origins of this principle reach back to antiquity: Shun rose from plowing and sowing to become emperor; the Great Yu personally plowed and came to possess All under Heaven; and the Zhou dynasty founded its state upon agriculture—Houji sent down the methods of sowing seed, Duke Liu (Gong Liu) was devoted to the affairs of the people, King Wen (Wenwang) applied himself to the work of the fields, and King Wu (Wuwang) attached great importance to the people's food. The rise of emperors and kings was always rooted in this. When King Cheng first assumed the reins of government, the Duke of Zhou composed the document "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi) to instruct him, which forms the counterpart to the ode "Seventh Month" (Qiyue)—how earnest and devoted was his loyalty and affection! Thereafter, King Cheng was able to follow his instruction, thereby achieving a governance of supreme harmony, extending the dynastic mandate for eight hundred years, and making Zhou the longest-reigning of the righteous dynasties of the Three Dynasties. King Wen, King Wu, and the Duke of Zhou had the means to found it, King Cheng and King Kang had the means to continue it, and the Dukes of Zhou and Shao had the means to [… 7 illegible characters].

Book of Odes (Shijing)
"Carefully arranged is the rabbit-net; hammered are its pegs, zheng-zheng! Stalwart is the martial man, a shield and wall for his prince! Carefully arranged is the rabbit-net, set in the middle of the thoroughfares. Stalwart is the martial man, a good companion for his prince! Carefully arranged is the rabbit-net, set in the middle of the forest. Stalwart is the martial man, the very heart and mind of his prince!"

Liu Chang 劉昌
Associate Examiner, Academician Reader-in-waiting Xi 習, comments: On this topic, the first stanza speaks of talent and the latter two stanzas speak of virtue; this essay may be said to have grasped this.
Examiner, Academician Expositor-in-waiting Ma 馬, comments: The reasoning and structure are smooth and clear, and the diction and tone are composed and unhurried; it is worthy of selection.
Examiner, Academician Qian 錢, comments: It skillfully depicts the flourishing of transformative governance and human talent in the house of Zhou; the phrasing is classical and elegant, and it deserves to be placed in the front ranks.

Having first drawn upon what he does to evoke that the man possesses usable talent, the poet again turns to what he does to evoke that the man possesses usable virtue. For talent is manifested on the outside, whereas virtue is harbored within. Now, since in […?] matters he is able to exercise such care, we know that this man is endowed with both talent and virtue—and how deep indeed is the way this is rooted in the moral transformation of King Wen! In antiquity, when King Wen governed the state, his transformative influence prevailed and customs became admirable; worthies and men of talent were numerous, so that even a rustic setting rabbit-nets possessed usable talent and virtue. Therefore, the poet praised him by drawing an evocative comparison from his task: saying that when he sets up that net, it is arranged with careful order; and when he hammers those pegs, there is a ringing sound, zheng-zheng. title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
城乎吾知其舉而用之必能捍衛乎國家藩屏乎王
室矣然此特以其才之見於外者言而未及乎德也
故又因事而言之若曰中逵中林皆施罝之所也罝
之施也雖非一二而所以為整飭之容則同地之易
也雖非一所而所以存敬謹之心則一惟其有敬謹
之德豈不可以為公侯好仇乎又豈不可以為公侯
腹心乎吾知其信而任之必能同功而一體同心而
同德矣吁椓杙也中逵也中林也其所寓不同而敬
謹之心惟隨寓而隨著干城也好仇也腹心也其所
===
用不同而才德之美必隨施而隨宜此可見賢才之
多而文王德化之盛極其至矣雖然論治化之盛必
本於人才論人才之盛必本於才德今兎罝野人而
其才德如此成周治化人才之盛可知宜詩人嘆美
之不已也
設業設虡崇牙樹羽應田縣鼓鞉磬柷圉既備乃
奏簫管備舉喤喤厥聲肅雝和鳴先祖是聽我
客戾止永觀厥成
劉昌

城乎？吾知其舉而用之，必能捍衛乎國家，藩屏乎王室矣。然此特以其才之見於外者言，而未及乎德也。故又因事而言之，若曰：中逵、中林，皆施罝之所也。罝之施也，雖非一二，而所以為整飭之容則同；地之易也，雖非一所，而所以存敬謹之心則一。惟其有敬謹之德，豈不可以為公侯好仇乎？又豈不可以為公侯腹心乎？吾知其信而任之，必能同功而一體，同心而同德矣。吁！椓杙也，中逵也，中林也，其所寓不同，而敬謹之心惟隨寓而隨著；干城也，好仇也，腹心也，其所用不同，而才德之美必隨施而隨宜。此可見賢才之多，而文王德化之盛極其至矣。雖然，論治化之盛，必本於人才；論人才之盛，必本於才德。今兎罝野人，而其才德如此，成周治化、人才之盛可知，宜詩人嘆美之不已也。

設業設虡，崇牙樹羽，應田縣鼓，鞉磬柷圉。既備乃奏，簫管備舉。喤喤厥聲，肅雝和鳴，先祖是聽。我客戾止，永觀厥成。
劉昌
translation_en:
…and wall? I know that if he is promoted and employed, he will certainly be able to defend the state and serve as a bulwark for the royal house. Yet this speaks only of his talent as manifested outwardly, without yet touching upon his virtue. Therefore, the poet again speaks of it through his work, as if to say: the crossroads and the deep forest are both places where the nets are set. Though the setting of nets is not done only once or twice, the orderly manner in which it is carried out is the same; though the changing of locations is not confined to a single place, the reverent and careful mind maintained throughout is one. Because he possesses this reverent and careful virtue, could he not serve as a good companion to a duke or marquis? And could he not also serve as the confidant of a duke or marquis? I know that if he is trusted and given responsibility, he will certainly be able to share in achievements as one body, and be of one mind and one virtue with his lord. Ah! Driving the pegs, at the crossroads, and in the deep forest—the circumstances in which he finds himself differ, yet his reverent and careful mind becomes manifest wherever it is placed; a shield and wall, a good companion, and a confidant—the ways in which he may be employed differ, yet the excellence of his talent and virtue is sure to be fitting however it is applied. From this we can see how numerous the worthy and talented were, and how the flourishing of King Wen's moral transformation reached its utmost height. Even so, in discussing the flourishing of governance and transformation, one must trace it to talented men; and in discussing the flourishing of talented men, one must trace it to their talent and virtue. Now, if even a rustic rabbit-netter possessed such talent and virtue as this, the flourishing of governance, transformation, and men of talent in the Zhou at its height can well be known; it is fitting indeed that the poet praised and admired him without cease.

"They set up the crossboards and the vertical posts, the upturned teeth and the upright plumes, the small and large hanging drums, the hand-drums, the chimes, the wooden starter, and the wooden stopper. When all are ready, the music begins; the panpipes and flutes are all raised together. Resounding are their tones, solemn and harmonious their notes; the ancestors listen to them. Our guests arrive, long to behold the complete performance."
Liu Chang

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
同考試官教諭董批此作理明詞贍善能形容周
人聲樂感通之妙宜在高選
考試官侍講學士馬批觀聲樂之備如在周庭
可謂善於形容者矣
考試官學士錢批理有發明文亦通暢佳作也
惟樂器備而聲無不和故神明格而人無不感夫神
人之感格者正以其樂備而聲和也苟不有樂器之
備而聲音之和則幽無以格乎神而又豈能明以感
乎人哉是詩說者謂周人始作樂而合祖也謂之設
===
業設虡則所以懸鍾磬者秩然而是陳也謂之崇牙
樹羽則所以飾業虡者粲然而可觀也業虡既設鍾
磬既懸以及小鼙而謂之應大鼓而謂之田又有周
制之縣鼓者焉固無一之不具矣柄而搖者為鞉石
而擊者為磬又有起樂止樂之柷敔者焉亦無一而
不備矣樂器固貴乎備備則斯奏焉簫管亦不可闕
既備斯舉焉于斯時也聲大而極其和者非喤喤厥
聲之謂乎音小而極其和者非肅雍和鳴之謂乎八
音之和如此豈不足以感格神人乎是故先祖者先

惟樂器備而聲無不和，故神明格而人無不感。夫神人之感格者，正以其樂備而聲和也。苟不有樂器之備而聲音之和，則幽無以格乎神，而又豈能明以感乎人哉？是詩，說者謂周人始作樂而合祖也。謂之「設業設虡」，則所以懸鍾磬者秩然而是陳也；謂之「崇牙樹羽」，則所以飾業虡者粲然而可觀也。業虡既設，鍾磬既懸，以及小鼙而謂之「應」，大鼓而謂之「田」，又有周制之「縣鼓」者焉，固無一之不具矣。柄而搖者為「鞉」，石而擊者為「磬」，又有起樂止樂之「柷敔」者焉，亦無一而不備矣。樂器固貴乎備，備則斯奏焉；簫管亦不可闕，既備斯舉焉。于斯時也，聲大而極其和者，非「喤喤厥聲」之謂乎？音小而極其和者，非「肅雍和鳴」之謂乎？八音之和如此，豈不足以感格神人乎？是故「先祖」者，先
translation_en:
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Dong: "This essay is clear in principle and rich in expression. It skillfully describes the wondrous efficacy of the Zhou people's music in moving and communicating [with spirits and men], and deserves to be placed high among the selections."
Comment by Examiner Academician Expositor-in-waiting Ma: "Reading of the completeness of the music and voices, one feels as if present in the court of Zhou. One may truly call this skillful in description."
Comment by Examiner Academician Qian: "The principles are well elucidated and the prose is fluent; a fine piece of work."
Only when musical instruments are complete are the sounds wholly harmonious; therefore the spirits are reached and no person is left unmoved. Indeed, the moving and reaching of spirits and men comes precisely from the music being complete and the sounds harmonious. Were there not the completeness of musical instruments and the harmony of sounds and tones, then in the unseen realm there would be no means to reach the spirits, and how in the visible realm could one move men? As for this ode, commentators say that when the Zhou people first created their music, they performed it jointly in the ancestral temple. When it speaks of "setting up the crossboards and setting up the upright posts," that by which the bells and chimes are suspended is arranged in orderly array; when it speaks of "the notched зуб-boards high above and the upright plumes," that by which the crossboards and upright posts are adorned is resplendent to behold. Once the crossboards and upright posts are set up and the bells and chimes suspended, down to the small drum called the ying, the large drum called the tian, and also the "suspended drum" of the Zhou institution—truly not a single one is lacking. That which has a handle and is shaken is the tao hand-drum; that which is made of stone and struck is the qing chime; and there are also the zhu wooden box and yu wooden tiger used to start and stop the music—here too not a single one is incomplete. Musical instruments are of course prized for their completeness, and once complete, they are played; the panpipes and double-pipes likewise cannot be omitted, and once everything is ready, they are taken up together. At such a moment, when the loud sounds reach the utmost harmony, is this not what is meant by "resounding is their sound"? When the subtler tones reach the utmost harmony, is this not what is meant by "solemn and harmonious is their blending"? With the eight timbres in such harmony as this, how could it fail to move and reach both spirits and men? Therefore, "the ancestors" are the former…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
王之神也於我有幽明之殊未易格焉今則洋洋在
上若有以聽我之樂而怨恫者無有也我客者夏商
之後也於我有疎遠之異不易感也今則顒顒在位
觀樂之成而厭斁者無有也謂之曰成者則與簫韶
九成為一致繹如也以成為不殊矣吁樂器兼大小
之備而無遺神人極感通之妙而無間非有周作樂
之盛能若是歟抑考虞書有曰祖考来格虞賓在位
商頌有曰我有嘉客亦不夷懌即此詩先祖是聽我
客戾止之謂也是知虞也商也周也時雖不同而音
===
樂之妙無不同世雖有異而感通之妙無或異所謂
先聖後聖其揆一也猗歟盛哉
春秋

王之神也，於我有幽明之殊，未易格焉。今則洋洋在上，若有以聽我之樂，而怨恫者無有也。我客者，夏、商之後也，於我有疎遠之異，不易感也。今則顒顒在位，觀樂之成，而厭斁者無有也。謂之曰「成」者，則與《簫韶》九成為一致，繹如也以成為不殊矣。吁！樂器兼大小之備而無遺，神人極感通之妙而無間，非有周作樂之盛，能若是歟？抑考《虞書》有曰：「祖考来格，虞賓在位。」《商頌》有曰：「我有嘉客，亦不夷懌。」即此詩「先祖是聽，我客戾止」之謂也。是知虞也、商也、周也，時雖不同，而音樂之妙無不同；世雖有異，而感通之妙無或異。所謂先聖後聖，其揆一也。猗歟盛哉！

《春秋》
「公及邾儀父盟于蔑。」「及宋人盟于宿。」〔隱元年〕「齊侯、鄭伯盟于石門。」〔三年〕「宋公、齊侯、衛侯盟于瓦屋。」〔八年〕「齊高子来盟。」〔閔二年〕「齊侯、宋公、江人、黃人盟于貫。」〔僖二年〕「盟于召陵。」〔四年〕「諸侯盟于首止。」〔五年〕「諸侯盟于葵丘。」〔九年〕
周鑑
translation_en:
…the spirits of the former kings. Between them and us lies the divide between the unseen and the seen, so they are not easily reached. Yet now they hover majestically above, as if listening to our music, with none bearing resentment or grief. "Our guests" are the descendants of the Xia and Shang dynasties. Between them and us lies the distance of estrangement, so they are not easily moved. Yet now they stand reverently in their places, observing the completion of the music, with none growing weary of it. Calling this a "completion" (cheng) means that it is at one with the nine movements of the Shao music (Xiaoshao jiucheng), and no different from "drawing it out to completion" (yi ru ye yi cheng). Ah! When musical instruments, both great and small, are provided without omission, and spirits and men reach the utmost marvel of sympathetic communion without a gap—if not for the flourishing creation of music by the house of Zhou, how could it be like this? Furthermore, if we examine the Book of Yu (Yushu), it says: "Progenitors and ancestors have come and arrived; the guest of Yu is in his place." And the Odes of Shang (Shangsong) say: "We have admirable guests; are they not also pleased and delighted?" This has the very same meaning as the lines in this ode: "The ancestors listen to it; our guests have arrived and stay." Thus we know that under Yu, Shang, and Zhou, although the times were different, the marvel of their music was no different; although the ages were distinct, the marvel of their sympathetic communion did not vary. As the saying goes, "Former sages and later sages, their principles are one." Oh, how magnificent!

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)
"The Duke and Yifu of Zhu made a covenant at Mie." "One of us and a man of Song made a covenant at Su." [First year of Duke Yin.] "The Marquis of Qi and the Earl of Zheng made a covenant at Shimen." [Third year.] "The Duke of Song, the Marquis of Qi, and the Marquis of Wei made a covenant at Wawu." [Eighth year.] "Master Gao of Qi came and made a covenant." [Second year of Duke Min.] "The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, a man of Jiang, and a man of Huang made a covenant at Guan." [Second year of Duke Xi.] "They made a covenant at Shaoling." [Fourth year.] "The feudal lords made a covenant at Shouzhi." [Fifth year.] "The feudal lords made a covenant at Kuiqiu." [Ninth year.]
By Zhou Jian 周鑑.

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
同考試官編脩江批公私之盟作者多失旨分截
不明此篇叙事不繁筆力老健非熟於春
秋者不能也一薦何忝
考試官侍講學士馬批議論正大得春秋之旨
考試官學士錢批題旨明而詞氣充必熟於比事之
教者宜在優等
講信屢出於私而春秋惡其非講信屢出於公而春
秋善其事夫盟春秋之所惡也與其盟而為私孰若
公天下之為愈哉先王盛時載誓掌於司盟非諸侯
所敢專也夫何魯隱即政之初首及附庸之邾而為
于蔑之盟再要三恪之微而為于宿之歃已而齊鄭
效尤於石門三國合黨於瓦屋列國紛紛始多故矣
然蔑之口血未乾宿之載牲即繼特盟之壇坫未掃
而參盟之要誓遽興朝盟而夕叛暫會而卒離無忠
信誠愨之心務衰世傾危之習是皆人心之私也春
秋惡之所以為王道計也吁盟固所當惡而又善其
事可乎有如齊桓主伯之時閔魯國之有難也高子
因奉使而為盟憤楚貢之不至也結江黃于貫盟屈

講信屢出於私，而《春秋》惡其非；講信屢出於公，而《春秋》善其事。夫盟，《春秋》之所惡也，與其盟而為私，孰若公天下之為愈哉！先王盛時，載誓掌於司盟，非諸侯所敢專也。夫何魯隱即政之初，首及附庸之邾而為于蔑之盟，再要三恪之微而為于宿之歃。已而齊、鄭效尤於石門，三國合黨於瓦屋，列國紛紛，始多故矣。然蔑之口血未乾，宿之載牲即繼；特盟之壇坫未掃，而參盟之要誓遽興。朝盟而夕叛，暫會而卒離，無忠信誠愨之心，務衰世傾危之習，是皆人心之私也。《春秋》惡之，所以為王道計也。吁！盟固所當惡，而又善其事可乎？有如齊桓主伯之時，閔魯國之有難也，高子因奉使而為盟；憤楚貢之不至也，結江、黃于貫，盟屈…
translation_en:
Associate Examiner and Historiographer (Bianxiu) Jiang comments: "Regarding covenants made for public versus selfish ends, most writers miss the point and fail to make clear structural divisions. This essay narrates events without wordiness and shows mature, vigorous brushwork. No one not thoroughly versed in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) could have produced it—how could there be any shame in recommending it?"

Examiner and Academician Expositor-in-Waiting (Shijiang xueshi) Ma comments: "The argument is upright and grand, grasping the essential meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals."

Examiner and Academician (Xueshi) Qian comments: "The theme of the topic is clear and the verbal force is full; the author must be well-versed in the teaching of 'comparing events' (bishi) and ought to be placed in the superior grade."

When pledges of good faith repeatedly sprang from selfish motives, the Spring and Autumn Annals condemned their wrongness; when pledges of good faith repeatedly sprang from public-mindedness, the Spring and Autumn Annals commended the deeds. Now, covenants are something that the Spring and Autumn Annals abhors; yet rather than entering into covenants for selfish ends, how much better is it to act for the public good of the world! In the flourishing age of the former kings, written oaths were in the charge of the Director of Covenants (Simeng) and were not something the feudal lords dared to usurp on their own authority. Why then, at the very beginning of Duke Yin of Lu's administration, did he first join with the dependency of Zhu to make the covenant at Mie, and then coerce a minor representative of the Three Revered Dynasties (Song) to smear blood in the covenant at Su? Soon afterward, Qi and Zheng imitated this wrongdoing at Shimen, and three states formed a partisan alliance at Wawu; the various states fell into turmoil, and troubles began to multiply. Yet before the sacrificial blood on their lips had dried at Mie, thevictim-bearing covenant at Su immediately followed; before the altars of bilateral covenants had been swept clean, the coerced oaths of tripartite covenants suddenly arose. They swore covenants in the morning and betrayed them in the evening; they met briefly and finally parted ways. Lacking hearts of loyalty, trustworthiness, and sincere uprightness, they pursued the treacherous and subversive habits of a declining age—all of this came from the selfishness of the human mind. The Spring and Autumn Annals condemned them in order to take counsel for the Kingly Way.

Alas! Since covenants ought indeed to be abhorred, how can one also commend such deeds? Take for instance the time when Duke Huan of Qi presided as Hegemon: commiserating with the state of Lu in its distress, Master Gao (Gaozi) made a covenant while serving as envoy; indignant that the tribute from Chu did not arrive, Duke Huan allied with Jiang and Huang at Guan, and made a covenant with Qu…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
完於召陵已而推戴王儲于首止申嚴五禁于葵丘
當時實有頼於桓矣然望國因之而綏靖荆楚由是
而帖服大本正於危疑之秋王法明於既晦之日收
人心於渙散扶衰世於小康事雖不請於司盟功實
有裨於中國是皆天下之公也春秋善之所以為世
道慮也嗟夫大道隱而家天下然後有誥誓忠信薄
而人心疑然後有詛盟盟詛煩而約劑亂末流不勝
其弊矣春秋惡其盟者盖欲革薄從忠有志於天下
為公之世也歟
===
春王正月〔隱元年〕城楚丘〔僖二年〕天王狩于河陽　公
朝于王所〔二十八年〕
第一場
同考試官教諭嚴　批春秋之作所以正王伯君臣之分
場中作者多失書法惟此得之故宜録出
考試官侍講學士馬　批属辭比事貴得其理此
篇鋪叙嚴整文有發明可取
考試官學士錢　批此篇斷制明白得春秋謹嚴之
旨高薦無忝

punctuated:
完於召陵，已而推戴王儲于首止，申嚴五禁于葵丘，當時實有頼於桓矣。然望國因之而綏靖，荆楚由是而帖服，大本正於危疑之秋，王法明於既晦之日，收人心於渙散，扶衰世於小康，事雖不請於司盟，功實有裨於中國，是皆天下之公也，《春秋》善之所以為世道慮也。嗟夫！大道隱而家天下，然後有誥誓；忠信薄而人心疑，然後有詛盟。盟詛煩而約劑亂，末流不勝其弊矣。《春秋》惡其盟者，盖欲革薄從忠，有志於天下為公之世也歟！
春王正月〔隱元年〕、城楚丘〔僖二年〕、天王狩于河陽，公朝于王所〔二十八年〕。
第一場。
同考試官教諭嚴批：《春秋》之作，所以正王伯、君臣之分。場中作者多失書法，惟此得之，故宜録出。
考試官侍講學士馬批：属辭比事，貴得其理。此篇鋪叙嚴整，文有發明，可取。
考試官學士錢批：此篇斷制明白，得《春秋》謹嚴之旨，高薦無忝。
translation_en:
… [Qu] Wan at Shaoling. Soon after, he upheld the royal heir-apparent at Shouzhi and solemnly proclaimed the five prohibitions at Kuiqiu; at that time, the realm truly depended upon Duke Huan. Yet because of this, the prestigious state [of Lu] was pacified and stabilized, and Jing-Chu was thereby brought into submissive obedience. The great foundation [of the royal succession] was rectified in an hour of peril and doubt, and the Kingly Law was made bright in a day when it had already grown dark. He gathered human hearts out of dispersion and propped up a declining age into a state of Lesser Tranquility. Even though these undertakings were not requested of the Director of Covenants (Simeng), their achievements genuinely benefited the Central States. All of this belonged to the public-mindedness of All under Heaven, and the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) approved of them out of concern for the Way of the world. Alas! Once the Great Way was obscured and All under Heaven was treated as a family possession, only then were there solemn announcements and oaths; once loyalty and trustworthiness grew thin and human hearts became suspicious, only then were there curses and covenants. When covenants and curses became frequent and written agreements fell into disorder, the degenerate course of later ages could no longer bear its own abuses. That the Spring and Autumn Annals detested their covenants was surely because it wished to reform superficiality and return to loyalty, aspiring toward an age in which All under Heaven is shared in common!

"In spring, the King's first month" [first year of Duke Yin]; "They walled Chuqiu" [second year of Duke Xi]; "The Heavenly King hunted at Heyang; the Duke had audience at the King's residence" [twenty-eighth year].

First Session.

Associate Examiner and Instructor (Jiaoyu) Yan comments: "The composition of the Spring and Autumn Annals was meant to rectify the distinctions between true king and hegemon, ruler and subject. Most writers in the examination compound missed the principles of its historiographical phrasing; this essay alone grasped them, and therefore ought to be selected for publication."

Examiner and Expositor-in-Waiting (Shijiang xueshi) Ma comments: "In linking words and arranging events for comparison, what is valued is grasping their underlying principle. This essay's exposition is rigorous and well-ordered, and the writing offers genuine elucidation; it is worthy of selection."

Examiner and Chancellor (Xueshi) Qian comments: "The judgments in this essay are clear and decisive, capturing the strict and solemn purport of the Spring and Autumn Annals; it is wholly deserving of high recommendation."

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
明王道而畧伯功尊君道而全臣禮此春秋之法也
嘅自黍離既降而雅頌不作聖人假魯史以寓王法
於一經之首即書春王正月意謂王不奉天則無以
行號令於天下諸侯不承王朔則無以立政教於國
中故書王次春書正次王言王必欽若天道諸侯必
謹守王度則大一統之義斯著而王道明矣惟其欲
明王道彼伯功雖大亦奚足取若衛為狄滅而齊桓
城楚丘以封之雖曰興滅繼絕然封國乃天子之大
權豈伯主所得專也春秋於此沒其迹而抑其事非
===
明王道而畧伯功者乎至若晉文自嫌強大召王就
見春秋乃書狩于河陽意謂周轍雖東猶為天下之
共主晉伯雖強不過列國之諸侯以臣召君其何以
訓用以天王自狩為文使天下咸知所尊而無敢不
敬則名分正而君道尊矣惟其欲尊君道故諸侯備
禮亦在所取若我公領袖乎列辟展敬於行在雖曰
所非其所然巡狩乃天子之大典朝覲適禮之變也
春秋於此諱其實而存其名非尊君道而全臣禮者
乎吁春秋之作在於尊君抑臣故畧伯主之專封者

punctuated: 明王道而畧伯功，尊君道而全臣禮，此《春秋》之法也。嘅自《黍離》既降而《雅》、《頌》不作，聖人假魯史以寓王法，於一經之首即書「春王正月」，意謂王不奉天，則無以行號令於天下；諸侯不承王朔，則無以立政教於國中。故書「王」次「春」，書「正」次「王」，言王必欽若天道，諸侯必謹守王度，則大一統之義斯著而王道明矣。惟其欲明王道，彼伯功雖大，亦奚足取？若衛為狄滅，而齊桓城楚丘以封之，雖曰興滅繼絕，然封國乃天子之大權，豈伯主所得專也？《春秋》於此沒其迹而抑其事，非明王道而畧伯功者乎？至若晉文自嫌強大，召王就見，《春秋》乃書「狩于河陽」，意謂周轍雖東，猶為天下之共主；晉伯雖強，不過列國之諸侯。以臣召君，其何以訓？用以天王自狩為文，使天下咸知所尊而無敢不敬，則名分正而君道尊矣。惟其欲尊君道，故諸侯備禮亦在所取。若我公領袖乎列辟，展敬於行在，雖曰「所」非其所，然巡狩乃天子之大典，朝覲適禮之變也。《春秋》於此諱其實而存其名，非尊君道而全臣禮者乎？吁！《春秋》之作，在於尊君抑臣，故畧伯主之專封者，
translation_en: To illuminate the Kingly Way and pass over the achievements of the hegemons, to exalt the Way of the Ruler and preserve intact the ritual propriety of subjects—this is the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). Alas, ever since the ode "Millet" (Shuli) was relegated to the Airs of the States and the Major and Minor Odes (Ya) and Hymns (Song) ceased to be composed, the Sage borrowed the history of Lu to lodge within it the Kingly Law. At the very beginning of the entire Classic, he immediately wrote, "Spring, the King's first month." His meaning was that if the King does not revere Heaven, he has no means by which to issue commands and orders to All Under Heaven; if the feudal lords do not receive the King's calendar, they have no means by which to establish governance and moral instruction within their states. Therefore, he wrote "King" after "Spring," and wrote "first [month]" after "King," meaning that the King must reverently accord with the Way of Heaven and the feudal lords must carefully abide by the King's regulations; then the principle of Grand Unity is made manifest and the Kingly Way is illuminated. Precisely because he wished to illuminate the Kingly Way, even though the achievements of those hegemons were great, how could they be worth commending? For instance, when Wei was destroyed by the Di tribes and Duke Huan of Qi walled Chuqiu in order to enfeoff it—although this was called reviving an extinguished state and continuing a severed line, the enfeoffment of states is nonetheless the great prerogative of the Son of Heaven; how could it be something a hegemon is permitted to monopolize? Here the Spring and Autumn Annals effaced the traces of who did it and suppressed the affair; is this not illuminating the Kingly Way and passing over the achievements of the hegemons? As for Duke Wen of Jin, suspecting his own great power, summoning the King to come for an audience, the Spring and Autumn Annals instead wrote, "[The Heavenly King] hunted at Heyang." The meaning was that even though the chariot tracks of Zhou had moved east, the King remained the common sovereign of All Under Heaven; and even though the Hegemon of Jin was strong, he was no more than a feudal lord among the various states. For a subject to summon his ruler—how could that serve as a precept? Therefore he phrased the text as though the Heavenly King had gone hunting of his own accord, causing All Under Heaven to know whom to revere and not dare to be disrespectful; thus names and statuses were rectified and the Way of the Ruler was exalted. Precisely because he wished to exalt the Way of the Ruler, when the feudal lords fulfilled ritual propriety, that too was something he commended. For instance, when our Duke [of Lu], taking the lead among the assembled lords, paid his respects at the temporary imperial quarters—although it was said that this "place" was not the proper place, a tour of inspection is nonetheless a great institution of the Son of Heaven, and paying court there was an adaptation of ritual to changing circumstances. Here the Spring and Autumn Annals concealed the reality of the matter while preserving its name; is this not exalting the Way of the Ruler and preserving intact the ritual propriety of subjects? Ah! The composition of the Spring and Autumn Annals lies in exalting the ruler and restraining the subject; therefore, in passing over the hegemon's unauthorized enfeoffment, …

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
學之設以教卿大夫元士之子與所升俊選之士比
年者每歲也中年則間一年也每歲皆有入學之人
既間一年必考之以觀其藝之進否若有人焉離絕
經書之句讀則必能辨别志向之邪正于以見其為
一年之所進也知謹於所習而不怠忽則能愛好同
類而無所暌貳又非其三年之所得乎再間而至於
五年觀其廣博所學而不拘於限制則必能親近師
長而於訓誨知嗜好矣又間而為七年觀其講求學
問討論蘊奧則必於取友輔仁知所擇矣然而至是
===
===
學則進矣而未幾乎老成行則脩矣而未安於純固
則可謂才之小成而未及乎成德也若夫積學於九
年之久考業於數四之餘則理明義精德盛仁熟其
於天下事物之理脩齊治平之道必能聞一以知十
因此而識彼觸類通達無所不知德性堅定卓然有
以自立而不為外物之所搖奪者是乃造乎成德之
地而為大成之士又豈一才一藝之可比哉抑考學
記一篇皆記先王作人之意上文言自家而國都莫
不有學則施教有其地矣此自一年以至九年皆有

… the University (Daxue) was established to instruct the sons of Ministers, Grandees, and Principal Servitors, along with the scholars of preeminent talent promoted from below. "Every year" means annually; "every other year" means after an interval of one year. In every year there were students who entered the school, and after an interval of one year, they were invariably examined to observe whether their skills had advanced or not. If there were those who could parse and punctuate the sentences of the classical texts, they would surely be able to distinguish between what was perverse and what was upright in their aspirations—by which one could see the progress they had made in the first year. Knowing how to be diligent in their studies without negligence, so that they could cherish their peers without estrangement or division—was this not what they attained by the third year? After another interval, reaching the fifth year, when one observed that they had broadened their learning without being bound by narrow limits, they would surely be able to draw close to their teachers and elders and take delight in their instruction. After yet another interval, at the seventh year, when one observed that they investigated learning and discussed its profound subtleties, they would surely know how to choose wisely in selecting friends to support their humane virtue. And yet at this point, although their learning had advanced, it did not yet approach mature perfection; although their conduct was cultivated, it did not yet rest in pure firmness. Thus it could be called the "minor accomplishment" of talent, not yet reaching perfected virtue.

As for accumulating learning over as long as nine years, after having had one's studies examined four times over, principles become clear and rightness refined, virtue abundant and humanity ripe. Regarding the principles of all things under heaven and the Way of self-cultivation, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world, such a person will surely be able to hear one thing and know ten, understand that from this, and comprehend by analogy until there is nothing he does not know. With a moral nature firm and settled, standing tall in self-reliance and unshaken by external things—this is indeed to reach the realm of perfected virtue and become a scholar of "great accomplishment." How could a mere single talent or single art be compared to this?

Moreover, if we examine the "Record on the Subject of Education" (Xueji) as a whole, it records throughout the former kings' intention in cultivating men of talent. text:

之才此所以治隆於上俗美於下而非後世之所能

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
於眾音之先商聲為臣而居次故作於宮音之後則
有以辨析乎君臣之分矣至若角次而為民徵羽為
事物皆以其象從而降殺則小大輕重之倫皆安其
位而不相奪高下疾徐之節各得其理而不相亂則
禮之天尊地卑之理貴賤以位之義豈不有以究其
精微之極通乎倫類之妙而謂之幾於禮者豈不信
乎雖然禮樂之道何嘗不貫通哉君子惟能審於聲
音達於政治辨義理之幾微明事物之纖悉則必致
樂以治心致禮以治躬而禮樂之理實有諸己夫有
===
諸己則其德之積於中者純然粹然而無一理之不
具睟面盎背而無一體之不充謂之曰德者得也言
必實得於己而非聲音笑貌之所為也故曰識乎聲
樂者斯通夫倫理之微明乎禮樂者必其有成德之
實者此也由是觀之樂必通乎禮而禮必寓於樂禮
也樂也乃政事之所關治道之所由成也君子苟不
能審於聲樂之間則倫理之幾微或不能辨矣又何
以有得於己而成其德也哉吁非知道者其孰能識
之
