音達於政治辨義理之幾微明事物之纖悉則必致
樂以治心致禮以治躬而禮樂之理實有諸己夫有
===
諸己則其德之積於中者純然粹然而無一理之不
具睟面盎背而無一體之不充謂之曰德者得也言
必實得於己而非聲音笑貌之所爲也故曰識乎聲
樂者斯通夫倫理之微明乎禮樂者必其有成德之
實者此也由是觀之樂必通乎禮而禮必寓於樂禮
也樂也乃政事之所關治道之所由成也君子苟不
能審於聲樂之間則倫理之幾微或不能辨矣又何
以有得於己而成其德也哉吁非知道者其孰能識
之
punctuated:
於眾音之先，商聲為臣而居次，故作於宮音之後，則有以辨析乎君臣之分矣。至若角次而為民，徵羽為事物，皆以其象從而降殺，則小大輕重之倫皆安其位而不相奪，高下疾徐之節各得其理而不相亂。則禮之天尊地卑之理、貴賤以位之義，豈不有以究其精微之極，通乎倫類之妙，而謂之幾於禮者，豈不信乎？
雖然，禮樂之道何嘗不貫通哉？君子惟能審於聲音，達於政治，辨義理之幾微，明事物之纖悉，則必致樂以治心，致禮以治躬，而禮樂之理實有諸己。夫有諸己，則其德之積於中者純然粹然，而無一理之不具；睟面盎背，而無一體之不充。謂之曰「德者，得也」，言必實得於己，而非聲音笑貌之所為也。故曰「識乎聲樂者斯通夫倫理之微，明乎禮樂者必其有成德之實」者，此也。
由是觀之，樂必通乎禮，而禮必寓於樂。禮也，樂也，乃政事之所關、治道之所由成也。君子苟不能審於聲樂之間，則倫理之幾微或不能辨矣，又何以有得於己而成其德也哉？吁！非知道者，其孰能識之？
translation_en:
…before all the other tones. The shang tone represents the minister and occupies the next position; thus it sounds after the gong tone, making it possible to distinguish the respective stations of ruler and minister. As for jue, which comes next and represents the people, and zhi and yu, which represent affairs and things, each descends in rank according to what it symbolizes. Thus the ordered relationships of greater and lesser, weightier and lighter, remain securely in their proper places without encroaching upon one another; and the measures of high and low, quick and slow, each accord with their proper principles without falling into disorder. Does this not enable one to fathom to their utmost refinement the ritual principle that Heaven is exalted and Earth lowly, and the meaning of noble and humble taking their respective places, and to comprehend the subtle ordering of relationships and categories? Is it not therefore true to say that such understanding approaches ritual propriety?
Yet when have the ways of ritual and music ever failed to interpenetrate? Only when the gentleman can discern sounds and tones, comprehend government, distinguish the subtlest workings of moral principles, and understand the finest details of affairs and things will he fully employ music to order his heart and ritual to regulate his person, so that the principles of ritual and music truly reside within him. When they reside within him, the virtue accumulated within is utterly pure and refined, lacking not a single principle. It shines in his face and fills out his bearing, leaving no part of his body unimbued. The saying “Virtue (de) is attainment (de)” means that one must truly attain it within oneself: it is not something produced by one's voice, smiles, or outward appearance. This is what is meant by saying, “Those who understand sounds and music thereby comprehend the subtleties of ethical relationships; those who understand ritual and music must possess the substance of perfected virtue.”
Viewed in this light, music necessarily communicates with ritual, and ritual necessarily resides within music. Ritual and music bear upon the affairs of government and are the means by which the way of good government is realized. If the gentleman cannot discern what lies within sounds and music, he may be unable to distinguish the subtlest workings of ethical relationships. How, then, could he attain them within himself and perfect his virtue? Ah! Who but one who knows the Way could understand this?

"Only the Most Sincere Can Establish the Great Foundation of the World"

Gao Lu 高輅

Associate Examiner, Historiographer (Bianxiu) Lai 賴 comments: "The topic of this discourse speaks fundamentally of human nature and principle, which is difficult to describe. If a composition [does not] err on the side of being roundabout, it errs on the side of being cursory. This essay is able to elucidate the topic concisely and pertinently; it is worthy of selection."

Examiner, Expositor-in-waiting (Shijiang xueshi) Ma 馬 comments: "The principles are clear and the diction is fluent, standing far above the crowd of compositions."

Examiner, Chancellor (Xueshi) Qian 錢 comments: "Throughout the discourse the writing brings forth genuine elucidation; he must be a scholar of broad learning."

The discourse reads: Only the sage reaches the ultimate of the virtue of utmost sincerity; therefore, he has that wherewith to encompass all the principles of the world. For utmost sincerity is that whereby the great foundation is established. Since the virtue of the sage has reached the ultimate of sincerity, how could the whole substance of his endowed nature not have that wherewith to encompass all the principles of the world? Allow me to expound upon this.

At birth, the sage is endowed with a disposition of keenness,明intelligence, and profound wisdom, and possesses the virtues of humanity, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, rising above the multitude of things and standing preeminent over all human relationships. As for his knowledge, he knows it from birth, attaining it without waiting upon thought; as for his practice, he practices it with ease, hitting the mark without waiting upon exertion. His physical endowment is clear and bright, all principles are completely present in him, and his virtue is genuine, real, and free from falsity. The Way of Heaven is utmost sincerity, profound and unceasing; the sage is pure in the Way of Heaven, and likewise is unceasing. Therefore, the text does not merely say "sincerity," but must say "the most sincere in the world," so as to show that nothing in the world can surpass the reality of the sage's virtue.

Because the virtue of the sage reaches the ultimate of sincerity and is free from falsity, how could there be even a single principle not completely present in the whole substance of his endowed nature? 君臣之敬而所以親所以敬者乃聖人性分之所存
夫婦之别長幼之序而所以别所以序者亦惟聖人
人道之所盡推之一事一物之間一言一行之際何
莫非出於聖人之性哉然聖人之性既有以統夫天

translation_en:
…proclaimed in Your Imperial utterance, seeking out the distant descendants of the Former Sage and bestowing upon me the emoluments and noble rank of an Arch-Duke. Your grace surpasses mountains and peaks, yet my repayment lacks even a drop of water or a speck of dust; assessing my station, how could I be worthy of this, and I engrave this gratitude upon my heart. What I pray is that cultural refinement may shine forth brightly, matching the radiance of the sun and moon, and that Your Sacred longevity may extend afar, enduring as long as Heaven and Earth. Overcome to the utmost with earnest emotion and reverent awe as I gaze up at Heaven and look upon Your Sacredness, I respectfully present this memorial of gratitude for Your Majesty's hearing.

===

第二問
同考試官編脩謝，批：性理之學，作者不少，但舉此遺彼者多矣。此篇條荅明白，非平日有講貫者不能也。
考試官侍講學士馬，批：辨析明暢，足破衆疑，蓋深於理學者也。

性一也，有自原於天而言者，有自賦於人而言者。原於天者，本然之理而無不善也；賦於人者，則氣質之拘，始有善惡之分焉。知乎此，則聖賢之論性可得而言矣。《商書》曰：「惟皇上帝，降衷于下民，若有恒性。」謂之
translation_en:
…entered, so that he was enfeoffed ahead of the other generals, enjoying wealth, honor, safety, and glory extending to his descendants, who held the titles of ranked marquises with fiefs stretching across prefectures and provinces, their blessings and good fortune enduring for generations—in this, [Deng] Yu 鄧禹 was the foremost. If those above, the officials and ministers, and those below, the common people, take to heart and personally practice all that is touched upon in the Sacred Instructions, then those who are ministers will have the means to fulfill their loyalty, those who are sons will have the means to fulfill their filial piety, and those who preserve benevolence in their hearts will love the people and extend that care to all things. This is truly how the Two Sages stimulate the conduct of the people and uphold the moral teachings of the world, thereby inaugurating an era of flourishing peace for ten thousand generations. To be born in this age and to be among these people—how fortunate indeed! I respectfully reply.

Second Question
Associate Examiner and Historiographer Xie [Xie Lian 謝璉] comments: Not a few writers have addressed the learning of human nature and principle, yet most cite one aspect while neglecting another. This essay answers point by point with clarity; none could produce it who had not thoroughly studied and mastered the subject in ordinary times.
Examiner and Expositor-in-Waiting Ma [Ma Yu 馬愉] comments: The analysis is clear and fluent, sufficient to dispel common doubts; clearly this is someone deeply versed in the learning of principle.
Examiner and Academician Qian [Qian Xili 錢習禮] comments: This policy essay answers every question as it is posed, dissecting the issues without omission; it is beyond the reach of ordinary compositions.

Human nature is one. Yet there are ways of speaking of it in terms of its origin in Heaven, and ways of speaking of it in terms of its endowment in human beings. That which originates in Heaven is original principle, and is in no respect not good; as for that which is endowed in human beings, constrained by physical temperament, a distinction between good and evil first arises therein. Once one understands this, the discussions of human nature by the sages and worthies can be spoken of. The Book of Shang (Shangshu) says: "The Great God (Huang Shangdi) has conferred even-handedness (zhong) on the inferior people, so that they comply with their constant nature." Why it is called…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
降衷者以天之降命於人而具以仁義禮知信之理
無所偏倚而人得以為常性也中庸曰天命之謂性
者謂天以陰陽五行化生萬物氣以成形而理亦賦
焉人物各得所賦之理以為健順五常之性也曰降
衷曰天命言之不同者衷但言人而命則兼乎物也
孔子易繫曰繼之者善成之者性而孟子專言性善
易繫蓋言人物未生之前而造化之理則謂之善人
物既生而各得其理則謂之性是善與性相對其言
善則重孟子以人之所受於天者言是所謂成之者
===
性而言善則輕言雖不同孟子之言實源於孔子非
有二本也至若荀卿之言性惡揚子之言善惡混韓
子之言性有三品皆以見於氣質者言而不知性之
本然其說固宜異矣近世儒者若眉山蘇氏則曰性
未有善惡得無近於揚子之說乎五峯胡氏曰性無
善惡又云謂之善者不過贊嘆之辭皆不能得其性
善之㫖但以理氣混而言之必如程子之言曰論性
不論氣不備論氣不論性不明二之則不是是也人
稟陰陽五行之理氣而生而有剛柔暴險智愚之不

punctuated: 降衷者，以天之降命於人，而具以仁義禮知信之理，無所偏倚，而人得以為常性也。《中庸》曰「天命之謂性」者，謂天以陰陽五行化生萬物，氣以成形，而理亦賦焉；人物各得所賦之理，以為健順五常之性也。曰「降衷」、曰「天命」，言之不同者，衷但言人，而命則兼乎物也。孔子《易繫》曰「繼之者善，成之者性」，而孟子專言「性善」。《易繫》蓋言人物未生之前，而造化之理則謂之善；人物既生，而各得其理，則謂之性。是善與性相對，其言善則重；孟子以人之所受於天者言，是所謂「成之者性」，而言善則輕。言雖不同，孟子之言實源於孔子，非有二本也。至若荀卿之言性惡，揚子之言善惡混，韓子之言性有三品，皆以見於氣質者言，而不知性之本然，其說固宜異矣。近世儒者，若眉山蘇氏，則曰「性未有善惡」，得無近於揚子之說乎？五峯胡氏曰「性無善惡」，又云「謂之善者，不過贊嘆之辭」，皆不能得其性善之㫖，但以理氣混而言之。必如程子之言曰：「論性不論氣，不備；論氣不論性，不明；二之則不是。」是也。人稟陰陽五行之理氣而生，而有剛柔暴險智愚之不
translation_en:
… "bestowing a moral sense" (jiangzhong 降衷) is because Heaven bestows its mandate upon humanity, endowing them with the principles of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness without the slightest partiality, which people thereby receive as their constant nature. When the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong 中庸) says, "What Heaven mandates is called nature," it means that Heaven generates and transforms the myriad things through yin and yang and the Five Phases; psychophysical force (qi 氣) forms their physical shapes, and principle (li 理) is also endowed therein, so that humans and things each obtain their endowed principle to serve as the nature of vigor,顺 docility, and the Five Constant Virtues. That one says "bestowing a moral sense" and the other says "Heaven's mandate"—the reason the expressions differ is that "moral sense" speaks only of humans, whereas "mandate" encompasses all things as well.

Confucius says in the Appended Remarks of the Book of Changes (Yi Xi 易繫), "What succeeds it is goodness; what completes it is nature," whereas Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) speaks exclusively of nature being good. The Appended Remarks of the Changes is speaking of the state before humans and things are born, when the principle of creative transformation is called "goodness"; once humans and things are born and each obtains its principle, it is called "nature." Thus, goodness and nature stand as correlatives, and the word "goodness" carries heavier weight. Mencius speaks in terms of what humans have received from Heaven, which corresponds to "what completes it is nature," and thus his use of the word "goodness" is lighter in scope. Although their expressions differ, Mencius's words actually originate from Confucius; they do not have two separate roots.

As for Xun Qing's (荀卿, Xunzi) claim that nature is evil, Master Yang's (Yangzi 揚子, Yang Xiong) claim that it is a mixture of good and evil, and Master Han's (Hanzi 韓子, Han Yu) claim that nature has three grades—all of these speak in terms of what is manifested in psychophysical endowment (qizhi 氣質) without knowing nature in its original state, so it is only natural that their doctrines should differ. Among scholars of recent ages, Master Su of Meishan (蘇氏, Su Shi) said that "nature does not yet have good or evil"—is this not close to Master Yang's theory? Master Hu of Wufeng (五峯胡氏, Hu Hong) said that "nature has neither good nor evil," and further stated that "calling it good is nothing more than an expression of praise and admiration." None of them were able to grasp the true purport of the goodness of nature, merely speaking of principle and psychophysical force as mixed together. Only the words of Master Cheng (Chengzi 程子)—"To discuss nature without discussing psychophysical force is incomplete; to discuss psychophysical force without discussing nature is unilluminating; to treat them as two separate things is wrong"—are right. Humans are born endowed with the principle and psychophysical force of yin, yang, and the Five Phases, and yet that there are inequalities of firmness and softness, violence and deviousness, wisdom and foolishness…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
一者誠由賦形受氣之時所稟有不同也故得陽氣
之多者則過於剛烈得陰氣之多者則過於柔弱躁
暴忿厲則為陽氣之惡狡譎姦險則為陰氣之惡若
其聖哲之流智慮明敏者非得夫氣之清乎下愚不
移善言難入者又非稟夫氣之濁乎且五常之謂性
孟子止言四端而朱子亦曰與之以仁義禮智之性
而皆不及信者盖有誠心為四端而信在其中矣故
五常之信猶五行之土無定位無成名無專氣而五
行無不待是以生也性發而為情中庸不曰性情而
===
曰中和盖中者無所偏倚所以狀性之德和者無所
乖戾所以著情之正中庸之言情四程子又謂其中
動而七情出焉盖中庸言情則其發於性之中者言
而程子則以外物觸之者不一而有此七情出也然
七情之於五性則哀喜愛欲者仁智之發怒與惡者
則義之著而懼非禮之所為乎未知是否惟執事
教之幸甚
第三問

一者誠由賦形受氣之時所禀有不同也故得陽氣
之多者則過於剛烈得隂氣之多者則過於柔弱躁
暴忿厲則爲陽氣之惡狡譎姦險則爲隂氣之惡若
其聖哲之流智慮明敏者非得夫氣之清乎下愚不
移善言難入者又非禀夫氣之濁乎且五常之謂性
孟子止言四端而朱子亦曰與之以仁義禮智之性
而皆不及信者盖有誠心爲四端而信在其中矣故
五常之信猶五行之土無定位無成名無專氣而五
行無不待是以生也性發而爲情中庸不曰性情而
===
曰中和盖中者無所偏倚所以狀性之德和者無所
乖戾所以著情之正中庸之言情四程子又謂其中
動而七情出焉盖中庸言情則其發於性之中者言
而程子則以外物觸之者不一而有此七情出也然
七情之於五性則哀喜愛欲者仁智之發怒與惡者
則義之著而懼非禮之所爲乎未知是否惟執事
教之幸甚
punctuated:
一者，誠由賦形受氣之時所稟有不同也。故得陽氣之多者，則過於剛烈；得陰氣之多者，則過於柔弱。躁暴忿厲，則為陽氣之惡；狡譎姦險，則為陰氣之惡。若其聖哲之流，智慮明敏者，非得夫氣之清乎？下愚不移，善言難入者，又非稟夫氣之濁乎？且五常之謂性，孟子止言四端，而朱子亦曰「與之以仁義禮智之性」，而皆不及信者，盖有誠心為四端，而信在其中矣。故五常之信，猶五行之土，無定位，無成名，無專氣，而五行無不待是以生也。性發而為情，《中庸》不曰性情而曰中和，盖中者無所偏倚，所以狀性之德；和者無所乖戾，所以著情之正。《中庸》之言情四，程子又謂「其中動而七情出焉」。盖《中庸》言情，則其發於性之中者言，而程子則以外物觸之者不一，而有此七情出也。然七情之於五性，則哀、喜、愛、欲者，仁、智之發；怒與惡者，則義之著；而懼，非禮之所為乎？未知是否，惟執事教之，幸甚。

第三問
translation_en:
…identical is truly because what they are endowed with at the moment they are given form and receive vital force (qi) differs. Therefore, those who obtain an abundance of yang vital force are overly rigid and fierce, while those who obtain an abundance of yin vital force are overly soft and weak. Impetuousness, violence, anger, and severity are the evils of yang vital force; craftiness, deceit, treachery, and险 [sinister]险ness are the evils of yin vital force. As for those among the sages and worthies whose wisdom and deliberation are bright and keen, have they not obtained the purity of vital force? And as for the lowest fools who do not change and whom good words scarcely penetrate, have they not been endowed with the turbidity of vital force? Furthermore, what is called human nature consists of the Five Constant Virtues, yet Mencius spoke only of the Four Beginnings, and Master Zhu [Zhu Xi] likewise said that Heaven "endows them with a nature of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom," neither mentioning trustworthiness (xin). This is because when there is a sincere heart acting as the Four Beginnings, trustworthiness is already contained within them. Thus, trustworthiness among the Five Constant Virtues is like Earth among the Five Phases: it has no fixed position, no established name of its own season, and no exclusive vital force, yet none of the Five Phases does not depend on it to come into being. When nature is aroused, it becomes the emotions. The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) does not speak of "nature and emotions" but of "equilibrium and harmony" (zhonghe). This is because equilibrium, being without inclination or deflection, describes the virtue of nature, while harmony, being without perversity or discord, manifests the correctness of the emotions. The Doctrine of the Mean speaks of four emotions [pleasure, anger, sorrow, and joy], whereas Master Cheng [Cheng Yi] further stated that "when the center is stirred, the seven emotions emerge from it." This is because when the Doctrine of the Mean speaks of the emotions, it refers to what issues from the equilibrium of nature, whereas Master Cheng refers to how external things stimulate it in varied ways, so that these seven emotions emerge. Yet as for how the seven emotions relate to the five virtues of nature: sorrow, joy, love, and desire are the issuance of benevolence and wisdom; anger and hatred are the manifestation of righteousness; and is not fear brought about by propriety? I do not know whether this is so or not; I would count myself most fortunate if Your Excellency would instruct me.

Third Question

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
同考試官給事中侯批五策隨問而荅此篇發明天人之道
尤明淨可觀
考試官侍講學士馬批策條荅有序文思可觀
考試官學士錢批此篇剖析詳明文詞簡潔必素有謀畧
可取
嘗謂三才之植立萬化之流行自一息至於不可終
窮自一毫至於不可限量所以綱維主宰者道而已
執事發策下詢承學以道為問甚盛心也敢不摭紀
載於經傳發明於儒先者以對粤稽諸易其繫辞曰
===
立天之道曰隂與陽立地之道曰柔與剛立人之道
曰仁與義天高地下人位乎中天之道既不出乎隂
陽地之道亦不出乎柔剛舎仁與義其何以立人之
道哉然聖人於斯道生而知之安而行之自然而然
者此聖人之德故子思謂誠者天之道賢人於斯道
學而知之利而行之使然而然者此賢人之學故子
思謂誠之者人之道雖不言地而本天而地在其中矣
中庸自二十一章而下至誠盡性而叅賛化育至誠
前知而先見如神博厚高明與天地悠久祖述憲章

道哉然聖人於斯道生而知之安而行之自然而然
者此聖人之德故子思謂誠者天之道賢人於斯道
學而知之利而行之使然而然者此賢人之學故子
思謂誠之者人之道雖不言地舉天而地在其中矣
中庸自二十一章而下至誠盡性而叅賛化育至誠
前知而先見如神博厚高明與天地悠久祖述憲章
punctuated:
同考試官給事中侯批：五策隨問而荅，此篇發明天人之道，尤明淨可觀。
考試官侍講學士馬批：策條荅有序，文思可觀。
考試官學士錢批：此篇剖析詳明，文詞簡潔，必素有謀畧，可取。
嘗謂：三才之植立，萬化之流行，自一息至於不可終窮，自一毫至於不可限量，所以綱維主宰者，道而已。執事發策，下詢承學，以道為問，甚盛心也。敢不摭紀載於經傳、發明於儒先者以對？粤稽諸《易》，其《繫辞》曰：「立天之道，曰隂與陽；立地之道，曰柔與剛；立人之道，曰仁與義。」天高地下，人位乎中。天之道既不出乎隂陽，地之道亦不出乎柔剛，舎仁與義，其何以立人之道哉？然聖人於斯道，生而知之，安而行之，自然而然者，此聖人之德，故子思謂「誠者天之道」；賢人於斯道，學而知之，利而行之，使然而然者，此賢人之學，故子思謂「誠之者人之道」。雖不言地，而本天而地在其中矣。《中庸》自二十一章而下，至誠盡性而叅賛化育，至誠前知而先見如神，博厚高明與天地悠久，祖述憲章…

Comment by Associate Examiner and Supervising Secretary Hou: The five policy essays answer each question in turn; this essay elucidates the Way of Heaven and humanity in a particularly clear, pure, and admirable manner.
Comment by Examiner and Expositor-in-Waiting Ma: The policy essay replies point by point in an orderly fashion, and its literary thought is admirable.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Qian: This essay analyzes the issues thoroughly and clearly, with concise and clean language; the candidate must long have possessed strategic insight. Acceptable.

I have always held that in the establishment of the Three Powers and the coursing of the myriad transformations, from a single breath to what cannot be exhausted, and from a single hair's breadth to what cannot be measured, that which serves as the overarching network and governing master is nothing other than the Way. For Your Excellency to set forth this policy question, inquiring of us junior scholars and asking about the Way, shows a most magnificent intention. How could I dare not gather what is recorded in the Classics and commentaries and elucidated by former Confucians in order to reply? Examining the Book of Changes (Yi), its "Appended Verbalizations" ("Xici") states: "What establishes the Way of Heaven is called yin and yang; what establishes the Way of Earth is called the soft and the firm; what establishes the Way of humanity is called benevolence and righteousness." Heaven is high and Earth is low, while humanity is positioned in the middle. Since the Way of Heaven does not go beyond yin and yang, and the Way of Earth likewise does not go beyond the soft and the firm, if one sets aside benevolence and righteousness, wherewith could one establish the Way of humanity? Yet in relation to this Way, the sage knows it from birth and practices it with ease; being so of itself, this is the virtue of the sage—hence Zisi 子思 said, "Sincerity is the Way of Heaven." The worthy, in relation to this Way, knows it through learning and practices it for its benefit; being made to be so through effort, this is the learning of the worthy—hence Zisi said, "The attainment of sincerity is the Way of humanity." Although Earth is not mentioned, it is rooted in Heaven and so Earth is included therein. In the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), from the twenty-first chapter onward: utmost sincerity fully realizes one's nature and assists in the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth; utmost sincerity foreknows and has godlike prescience; breadth, thickness, height, and brilliance are enduring along with Heaven and Earth; transmitting the past and modeling on the statutes…

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
與天地同德聰明睿知而極博厚淵泉之盛經綸立
本而有其淵其天之妙此自誠明之事自然而然者
豈非天道之謂乎致曲而至於有誠成己而及於成
物尊德性充其道之大道問學盡其道之小愚不用
賤不專而為下不倍本諸身徵諸民而在上不驕此
自明誠之事使然而然者豈非人道之謂乎至於問
仁釋克己復禮為乾道顏子資質剛明此乾道奮發
而有為以主敬行恕為坤道仲弓資質温粹此坤道
靜重而持守夫子各因其材而篤之亦皆使然而然
===
人之道也中庸以知之至行之盡而道在聖人故謂
聖人之道王天下有三重本諸身者有其德以居其
位故謂君子之道至於堯舜之孝弟夫子之忠恕皆
謂而已矣者固竭盡無餘之詞又有謂為士之次違
道不遠異者堯舜人倫之至此全體之孝弟士但能
不失其良心而已此一節之孝弟夫子一理渾然泛
應曲當此聖人之忠恕學者必盡己推己以求聖人
之道此學者之忠恕道在天下人皆可以與知能行若推
其極雖聖人亦不能加毫末於其間也豈有二理乎哉謹對

punctuated: 與天地同德，聰明睿知而極博厚淵泉之盛，經綸立本而有其淵其天之妙：此自誠明之事，自然而然者，豈非天道之謂乎？致曲而至於有誠，成己而及於成物，尊德性充其道之大，道問學盡其道之小，愚不用、賤不專而為下不倍，本諸身、徵諸民而在上不驕：此自明誠之事，使然而然者，豈非人道之謂乎？至於問仁，釋「克己復禮」為乾道，顏子資質剛明，此乾道奮發而有為；以「主敬行恕」為坤道，仲弓資質温粹，此坤道靜重而持守。夫子各因其材而篤之，亦皆使然而然，人之道也。《中庸》以知之至、行之盡而道在聖人，故謂「聖人之道」；王天下有三重，本諸身者有其德以居其位，故謂「君子之道」。至於堯、舜之孝弟，夫子之忠恕，皆謂「而已矣」者，固竭盡無餘之詞，又有謂為「士之次」、「違道不遠」異者：堯、舜人倫之至，此全體之孝弟，士但能不失其良心而已，此一節之孝弟；夫子一理渾然，泛應曲當，此聖人之忠恕，學者必盡己推己以求聖人之道，此學者之忠恕。道在天下，人皆可以與知能行，若推其極，雖聖人亦不能加毫末於其間也。豈有二理乎哉？謹對。
translation_en:
… matching the virtue of Heaven and Earth; possessing intelligence, perspicacity, and wisdom that reach the utmost fullness of breadth, depth, and springing abysses; ordering the great warp of the world and establishing the great foundation while possessing the subtlety of the abyss and of Heaven: these are the affairs of proceeding from sincerity to enlightenment, things that are so of themselves—is this not what is meant by the Way of Heaven? Pushing partial goodness to the utmost until one possesses sincerity; completing oneself and extending to the completion of things; honoring one's virtuous nature to fill out the greatness of the Way, and pursuing inquiry and study to exhaust the finest details of the Way; being ignorant and therefore not self-reliant, being lowly and therefore not presumptuous, so that in a subordinate position one is not rebellious; grounding it in one's own person and verifying it among the common people, so that in a superior position one is not arrogant: these are the affairs of proceeding from enlightenment to sincerity, things made to be so through effort—is this not what is meant by the Way of Man?

As for the inquiries about benevolence (ren), [Master Zhu] explains "overcoming the self and returning to ritual propriety" as the Way of Qian (Heaven): Master Yan [Yan Hui 顏回] had a disposition that was firm and clear, and this is the Way of Qian, rousing itself to vigorous action. He takes "holding fast to reverence and practicing reciprocity" as the Way of Kun (Earth): Zhonggong [Ran Yong 冉雍] had a disposition that was gentle and pure, and this is the Way of Kun, tranquil, weighty, and steadfastly preserving. The Master [Confucius] encouraged each according to his natural capabilities; both are likewise things made to be so through effort, which is the Way of Man.

Because the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) holds that when knowledge reaches its utmost and practice is exhausted, the Way resides in the sage, it calls this "the Way of the Sage." Because ruling the world as true king involves three important matters, and he who grounds them in his own person possesses both the virtue and the position, it calls this "the Way of the Superior Man."

As for the filial piety and fraternal submission of Yao and Shun, and the conscientiousness and reciprocity (zhongshu) of the Master [Confucius], both are spoken of with the phrase "and that is all," which is assuredly an expression indicating complete exhaustion with nothing left over. Yet the reason they differ from what are elsewhere called "the next tier of scholar-official" and "not far from the Way" is this: Yao and Shun were the culmination of human relationships, and theirs was filial piety and fraternal submission in its entire substance, whereas the scholar-official is merely able not to lose his innate good conscience, which is filial piety and fraternal submission in a single aspect; the Master possessed the one principle in undivided wholeness, responding broadly and fittingly to every turn, which is the conscientiousness and reciprocity of the sage, whereas the learner must exhaust himself and extend from himself to others in order to seek the Way of the Sage, which is the conscientiousness and reciprocity of the learner.

The Way is present throughout the world; all people can share in knowing it and being able to practice it. Yet if one pushes it to its ultimate perfection, even a sage cannot add a hair's breadth to it. How could there be two distinct principles? I respectfully reply.

陳雲鵬

古之士也寘之選列孰曰不宜

自古帝王之御世也必以教民為先而教民之道必
以學校為務學校既興則可以敦化為善俗矣稽之
三代夏曰校殷曰序周曰庠皆鄉學也國都之學皆
===

養老習射受脤獻馘皆在焉而其教也八歲入小學
十五入大學有六德六行為之本又以六藝習其文
其不率教則有八刑之糾焉當時天子公卿躬行於

translation_en:
Fourth Policy Question
Chen Yunpeng 陳雲鵬
Comment by Associate Examiner Instructor Liu 劉: "He is able to give a detailed and thorough account of the school systems of successive dynasties, and furthermore offers sound arguments, like a scholar of antiquity. If we place him in the ranks of the selected, who would say it is inappropriate?"
Comment by Examiner Academician Expositor-in-waiting Ma 馬: "The policy essay is grounded in historical evidence and merits selection."
Comment by Examiner Academician Qian 錢: "The evidential research is clear and the literary expression is well-ordered; throughout [?] it is superior."

Since antiquity, when emperors and kings have governed the world, they have invariably made instructing the people their first priority; and in the way of instructing the people, they have invariably made schools their central task. Once schools flourish, moral transformation can be deepened and customs made good. Examining the Three Dynasties, in the Xia it was called xiao 校, in the Yin it was called xu 序, and in the Zhou it was called xiang 庠—all of these were local schools; the schools in the capital were in all cases called xue 學. The Yin further designated the Great Learning (daxue 大學) as the School of the Right (youxue 右學) and the Elementary Learning (xiaoxue 小學) as the School of the Left (zuoxue 左學), also called the Hall of the Blind Musicians (guzong 瞽宗). The Zhou designated the Great Learning as the Eastern School (dongjiao 東膠) and the Elementary Learning as the Yu School (yuxiang 虞庠). All of these served to instruct the sons and younger brothers of the state, and the rites of nourishing the aged, practicing archery, receiving sacrificial meat before a campaign, and presenting the severed left ears of slain enemies were all performed therein. As for their instruction, at eight years of age one entered the Elementary Learning, and at fifteen one entered the Great Learning. There were the Six Virtues and Six Conducts to serve as its foundation, and the Six Arts to practice its refinement; for those who did not follow instruction, there was correction by the Eight Punishments. At that time, the Son of Heaven and the dukes and ministers personally practiced virtue above, so that their words, deeds, and administrative affairs could all serve as models. Therefore, the people of the Three Dynasties walked the straight Way, and customs were exceedingly fine. When the Han arose, succeeding to the remnant decline and disorder of the Qin, its institutions were roughly improvised and there was not yet leisure for the business of schools. In the time of Emperor Xiaowen, Wen Wong 文翁 established schools in Shu 蜀, which was limited to a single commandery; yet commentators say that from Emperors Gao 高 and Hui 惠 down to Wen 文 and Jing 景, the common people were simple and honest, and punishments were almost set aside entirely. 納董仲舒之言立太學及郡國學用田蚡為相黜黃
老刑名百家之言延儒者以百數各以經授徒名亦
美矣而其實則未有焉光武中興崇重儒術首建太
學稽式古典脩明禮樂明帝尊師重傅臨雍拜老期
門羽林之士悉通經義又為樊郭陰馬立四姓小侯
學而郡國之學亦嘗舉焉西漢尚經術由於武帝用
公孫弘之徒東漢尚風節由於光武物色嚴光之流
之所為也至於唐太宗大召名儒增廣生員增築學
===
舍千二百間又設六學皆隸國子監生徒皆有數國
子生三百人大學五百人四門學三百人律學五十
人書學筭學各三十人以及屯營飛騎皆給博士授
經外國皆遣子入學鼓篋踵堂者至八千餘人學校
之盛自漢以来未之有也當時斗米三錢外戶不閉
亦其富而教之時矣而躬行則有未至士習之流徒
以詞章為尚而無益於風俗也逮至有宋太祖初開
國子監數臨幸焉當時州縣學雖未遍立而儒者往
往依山林間講授大率多至數百十人有若嵩陽嶽

punctuated: 然者，由於高、惠之寬仁，文、景之恭儉以致之也。武帝納董仲舒之言，立太學及郡國學，用田蚡為相，黜黃老、刑名百家之言，延儒者以百數，各以經授徒，名亦美矣，而其實則未有焉。光武中興，崇重儒術，首建太學，稽式古典，脩明禮樂。明帝尊師重傅，臨雍拜老，期門、羽林之士悉通經義，又為樊、郭、陰、馬立四姓小侯學，而郡國之學亦嘗舉焉。西漢尚經術，由於武帝用公孫弘之徒；東漢尚風節，由於光武物色嚴光之流之所為也。至於唐太宗大召名儒，增廣生員，增築學舍千二百間，又設六學，皆隸國子監，生徒皆有數：國子生三百人，大學五百人，四門學三百人，律學五十人，書學、筭學各三十人；以及屯營飛騎，皆給博士授經，外國皆遣子入學，鼓篋踵堂者至八千餘人。學校之盛，自漢以来未之有也。當時斗米三錢，外戶不閉，亦其富而教之時矣，而躬行則有未至，士習之流，徒以詞章為尚，而無益於風俗也。逮至有宋，太祖初開國子監，數臨幸焉。當時州縣學雖未遍立，而儒者往往依山林間講授，大率多至數百十人，有若嵩陽、嶽
translation_en: … was so was because it was brought about by the broad benevolence of Emperors Gaozu and Hui, and the reverence and frugality of Emperors Wen and Jing. Emperor Wu accepted the counsel of Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒, established the Imperial University (Taixue) as well as schools in the commanderies and principalities, employed Tian Fen 田蚡 as Counselor-in-Chief, dismissed the doctrines of Huang-Lao, Forms and Names (Legalism), and the Hundred Schools, and invited Confucian scholars by the hundreds, each teaching the Classics to disciples. In name this was admirable indeed, yet the reality was not there. With the restoration under Emperor Guangwu, Confucian learning was venerated and esteemed; he first established the Imperial University, investigated and modeled his institutions on ancient canons, and cultivated and clarified ritual and music. Emperor Ming honored teachers and revered tutors, visited the Hall of the Circular Moat (Biyong) to pay homage to the aged, ensured that theGentlemen of the Palace Gate (Qimen) and As Rapid as Tigers (Yulin) imperial guards were all conversant with the meanings of the Classics, and furthermore established a school for the "Little Marquises" of the Four Surnames—the Fan 樊, Guo 郭, Yin 陰, and Ma 馬 clans—while schools in the commanderies and principalities were also promoted. That the Western Han esteemed classical scholarship resulted from what Emperor Wu did in employing the likes of Gongsun Hong 公孫弘; that the Eastern Han esteemed moral integrity resulted from what Emperor Guangwu did in seeking out the likes of Yan Guang 嚴光. Coming to Emperor Taizong of the Tang, he summoned renowned Confucian scholars on a grand scale, expanded the quotas of students, built an additional twelve hundred bays of school dormitories, and also established the Six Schools, all subordinate to the Directorate of Education (Guozijian), each with a fixed quota of students: three hundred students in the School for the Sons of the State (Guozixue), five hundred in the National University (Taixue), three hundred in the School of the Four Gates (Simenxue), fifty in the Law School (Lüxue), and thirty each in the Calligraphy School (Shuxue) and Mathematics School (Suanxue). Even the garrisoned Flying Cavalry (Feiqi) guards were all provided with Erudites (Boshi) to instruct them in the Classics, and foreign states all sent their sons to enroll in the schools, so that those who beat the drum to open their book-boxes and followed one another’s heels into the lecture halls reached more than eight thousand men. Such flourishing of schools had never been seen since the Han dynasty. At that time, a peck of rice cost three cash and outer doors were left unbolted—it was truly a time for educating the people after enriching them. Yet in personal practice on the part of the ruler there were still shortcomings, so that the trend among literati practices merely valued belles-lettres and was of no benefit to public customs. Down to the Song dynasty, Emperor Taizu first opened the Directorate of Education and visited it in person several times. At that time, although prefectural and county schools had not yet been established everywhere, Confucian scholars often relied on mountain and forest retreats to lecture and teach, generally gathering as many as several dozen or several hundred students, such as the Songyang 嵩陽, Yuelu 嶽…

text:
□□睢陽四書院焉□□真宗景德中始賜九經
于州縣學及講授之所至仁宗慶曆間范仲淹言欲
復古勸學而取人必本行實歐宋諸公亦言士必土
著而教之而後州縣察其履行而舉之州縣之學於
是皆立矣然當時士尚忠厚真儒輩出卒以接絕學
於千載之上而風化之盛幾於三代也然則風俗之
厚實本於學校之興尤有本於上之躬行以致之管
見如是幸執事教之
第五問
===
李庸脩
同考試官侍讀習批所荅簡而明潔殊異雜作
考試官侍講學士馬批策有考據善荅所問有識之士也
考試官學士錢批此策所問場中多不能記汎舉以對惟
此篇於先儒之言皆有所考尤為傑作
嘗謂國家得賢以成治功賢才用世而著勛烈故有
一代之興必有一代之臣推之往昔盖可見矣執事
發策以漢唐宋人臣之賢者為問敢不歷舉以對炎
漢之興明辨達理以竒謀至計佐高祖成帝業平生

punctuated:
□□、睢陽四書院焉。□□真宗景德中，始賜九經于州縣學及講授之所。至仁宗慶曆間，范仲淹言欲復古勸學，而取人必本行實。歐宋諸公亦言士必土著而教之，而後州縣察其履行而舉之。州縣之學於是皆立矣。然當時士尚忠厚，真儒輩出，卒以接絕學於千載之上，而風化之盛幾於三代也。然則風俗之厚，實本於學校之興，尤有本於上之躬行以致之。管見如是，幸執事教之。
第五問
李庸脩
同考試官侍讀習批：所荅簡而明潔，殊異雜作。
考試官侍講學士馬批：策有考據，善荅所問，有識之士也。

嘗謂國家得賢以成治功，賢才用世而著勛烈。故有一代之興，必有一代之臣，推之往昔，盖可見矣。執事發策，以漢唐宋人臣之賢者為問，敢不歷舉以對？炎漢之興，明辨達理，以竒謀至計佐高祖成帝業，平生
translation_en:
…[two illegible characters] and Suiyang—the four academies. [Two illegible characters] During Emperor Zhenzong’s Jingde era, copies of the Nine Classics first began to be bestowed upon prefectural and county schools and places of instruction. In Emperor Renzong’s Qingli era, Fan Zhongyan argued that, to restore ancient practices and encourage learning, the selection of men for office must rest upon their actual conduct. Masters Ou and Song likewise argued that scholars must be established residents of their localities and receive instruction there; only then should prefectural and county authorities examine their conduct and recommend them. Schools were consequently established throughout the prefectures and counties. Scholars at that time esteemed loyalty and generosity, and true Confucians emerged in succession. They ultimately renewed the transmission of learning that had been broken off more than a thousand years earlier, and the flourishing of moral influence nearly equaled that of the Three Dynasties. Thus, the soundness of customs truly rests upon the flourishing of schools, and still more fundamentally upon the ruler’s personal practice that brings it about. Such is my limited view; I hope that you will favor me with instruction.
Fifth Question
Li Yongxiu

title: 正統十年會試錄
text:
功利不係於心主雖輕士善罵敬之不敢慢順之不
最强的明哲保身此子房所以優於三傑也正誼
明道學術純正君子謂漢廷大臣攻君之過禁君之
欲固有其人求其大正君心引之志於仁者董仲舒
其庶幾乎正直忠厚足以闢公孫弘之阿諛張湯之
殘刻至使淮南寢謀武帝亦敬憚之謂古有社稷臣
汲黯近之當漢末造三方鼎峙立國西蜀規取中原
復漢討賊以伸大義其心未嘗一日忘凡其所立之
竒偉者惟以廣忠思集眾益開誠心布公道四者為
===
之本此諸葛武侯誠一世之人龍也魏鄭公忠亮自
任佐主於維新之朝犯顏强諫瀕死不悔致君能用
其言成貞觀之治以功名終陸宣公諳練治體從主
於艱虞之際知無不言言無不盡曲折調護以脫奉
天之難不恤其身范文正才氣老成素負先憂後樂
之志世皆仰其為第一流人及至登用奮見有為屢
遭屈抑而不挫大厲名節振作士大夫之功為多韓
忠獻識量英偉平生喜慍不形諸色兩定大計國家
危疑身任其責知無不為不以豫憂利害而輟卒安

punctuated: 功利不係於心。主雖輕士善罵，敬之不敢慢，順之不最强的，明哲保身，此子房所以優於三傑也。正誼明道，學術純正，君子謂漢廷大臣攻君之過、禁君之欲，固有其人，求其大正君心、引之志於仁者，董仲舒其庶幾乎！正直忠厚，足以闢公孫弘之阿諛、張湯之殘刻，至使淮南寢謀，武帝亦敬憚之，謂「古有社稷臣，汲黯近之」。當漢末造，三方鼎峙，立國西蜀，規取中原，復漢討賊，以伸大義，其心未嘗一日忘。凡其所立之竒偉者，惟以廣忠思、集眾益、開誠心、布公道四者為之本，此諸葛武侯誠一世之人龍也。魏鄭公忠亮自任，佐主於維新之朝，犯顏强諫，瀕死不悔，致君能用其言，成貞觀之治，以功名終。陸宣公諳練治體，從主於艱虞之際，知無不言，言無不盡，曲折調護，以脫奉天之難，不恤其身。范文正才氣老成，素負「先憂後樂」之志，世皆仰其為第一流人。及至登用，奮見有為，屢遭屈抑而不挫，大厲名節，振作士大夫之功為多。韓忠獻識量英偉，平生喜慍不形諸色，兩定大計，國家危疑，身任其責，知無不為，不以豫憂利害而輟，卒安
translation_en:
…thoughts of personal credit and profit never attached to his mind. Even though his sovereign belittled scholars and was prone to cursing them, he treated Zifang [Zhang Liang 張良] with respect and dared not slight him, yielding to him and not [?] [OCR garble for 敢強之, "daring to force him"]. Wise and discerning in preserving his own person—this is why Zifang was the finest of the Three Heroes.

Rectifying righteousness and clarifying the Way, his scholarly learning was pure and orthodox. Gentlemen have said that among the great ministers of the Han court, there were indeed those who attacked the sovereign's faults and curbed the sovereign's desires; yet if one seeks someone who fundamentally rectified the sovereign's heart and guided his aspirations toward benevolence, Dong Zhongshu 董仲舒 came close indeed!

Upright and loyally generous, he was able to expose the sycophancy of Gongsun Hong 公孫弘 and the ruthless harshness of Zhang Tang 張湯, to the point of causing the King of Huainan 淮南 to abandon his rebellious plots. Even Emperor Wu 武帝 respected and held him in awe, declaring, "In antiquity there were ministers of the altars of state; Ji An 汲黯 comes close to this."

At the end of the Han, when three powers stood like the legs of a tripod, he established a state in western Shu 蜀 and planned the recovery of the Central Plains, seeking to restore the Han and punish the traitors so as to uphold great righteousness—a purpose his heart never forgot for a single day. In all the extraordinary and great achievements he established, he took as his foundation solely the four principles of broadening loyal thought, gathering collective benefit, opening an honest heart, and spreading the public Way. Thus Zhuge, Marquis Wu 諸葛武侯 [Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮], was truly the "dragon among men" of his age.

Wei, Duke Zheng 魏鄭公 [Wei Zheng 魏徵], took loyal integrity as his personal duty and assisted his sovereign in a court of renewal. He braved the imperial countenance to offer forceful remonstrance, without regret even when close to death, bringing his ruler to heed his words, achieving the good governance of the Zhenguan 貞觀 era (627–649), and ending his life with merit and renown.

Lu, Duke Xuan 陸宣公 [Lu Zhi 陸贄], was thoroughly versed in the principles of governance. Following his sovereign in a time of hardship and peril, he spoke of all that he knew and held nothing back in his words, mediating and protecting with intricate care to deliver the emperor from the crisis at Fengtian 奉天 without regard for his own person.

Fan Wenzheng 范文正 [Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹] possessed mature talent and spirit, and had long cherished the aspiration to "worry before the world worries and rejoice after the world rejoices," so that the world looked up to him as a man of the very first rank. When he was promoted and employed, he roused himself to vigorous action; though repeatedly subjected to frustration and suppression, he was never broken, greatly sharpening integrity and honor and accomplishing much in rousing the spirit of the scholar-officials.

Han Zhongxian 韓忠獻 [Han Qi 韓琦] possessed heroic and grand insight and capacity; throughout his life, joy and anger never showed upon his face. Twice he settled the great plans of succession. text:
社稷德業盛大求之古人無少愧焉司馬文正恭儉
正直終身語未嘗妄容人盡言雖忤之而不慍誠出
自然遠夷畏服晚登相位更張新法民之老稚交口
稱快如獲更生君子稱其有旋乾轉坤之功非虚語
也謹以是復明問未知是否裁之幸甚

punctuated: 社稷，德業盛大，求之古人無少愧焉。司馬文正恭儉正直，終身語未嘗妄，容人盡言，雖忤之而不慍，誠出自然，遠夷畏服。晚登相位，更張新法，民之老稚交口稱快，如獲更生。君子稱其有旋乾轉坤之功，非虚語也。謹以是復明問，未知是否，裁之幸甚。
translation_en: … the altars of soil and grain; his virtuous achievements were grand and great, and even if measured against the ancients, he would have nothing to be ashamed of. Sima Wenzheng (Sima Guang 司馬光) was respectful, frugal, and upright. Throughout his life he never spoke falsely, and he tolerated others speaking their minds fully, never growing angry even when they offended him. His sincerity arose naturally, so that even distant foreign peoples held him in awe and submitted to him. Late in life he ascended to the position of Grand Councilor and overhauled the New Policies; among the common people, old and young alike vied to voice their delight, feeling as though they had been given a new lease on life. When superior men praised him for having the merit of turning heaven and earth around, these were no empty words. I respectfully offer this in reply to your enlightened question; not knowing whether it is right or wrong, I would be most fortunate if you would judge it.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

The flourishing of governance and moral transformation is bound up with the flourishing of the cosmic dispensation; yet it also depends upon a multitude of worthy talents assisting together in bringing it to completion. And the emergence of worthy talents, in turn, is rooted in the ruler above renewing and inspiring them so as to bring this about. When the Book of Documents (Shu) speaks of "men of eminence and ability being in office," it necessarily stems from Emperor Shun's "receiving them all and widely employing them"; when the Book of Odes (Shi) sings of "the stately multitude of officers," it necessarily originates from King Wen's "making famous and accomplished these officers." Our dynasty has received the bright mandate of Heaven, its fortune meeting with an era of prosperity and excellence. Literary and moral teaching greatly flourishes, and political transformation is pure and harmonious. Within and beyond the seas, all give rise to the wish to be ministers of the Emperor, without distinction even in distant and secluded regions—how could this come about without a source? We reverently reflect how His Majesty has succeeded to the line of the Successive Sacred Emperors, further broadening transformative governance. At the very beginning of his succession to the great royal heritage, he attended the Classics Mat (jingyan) to expound learning and discuss the Way, growing ever more diligent day and night, …

translation_en:
…He personally inspected the Directorate of Education and offered sacrificial libations to the Former Teacher Confucius, venerating the Way of the Sages. He has repeatedly issued imperial commands to the authorities throughout the realm to supervise and encourage educational administration, so as to inspire and rouse the community of scholars. Therefore, those who are scholars have all been moved to gratitude and have honed themselves, striving to rise to service; those who wish to establish achievements and leave behind a glorious reputation for eternity emerge in great refinement and abundance. The multitude of these men of talent is sufficient to rival the courts of Yu and Zhou, and it is fitting that the flourishing of His transformative governance also matches the splendor of the ages of Yu and Zhou.

In the second month of spring in the yichou year of the Zhengtong reign (1445), one thousand two hundred tribute scholars from across the realm presented themselves for examination at the Ministry of Rites. When the time arrived, the Minister, Your Servant [Hu] Ying 胡濙, petitioned for the appointment of Examiners, and His Majesty the Emperor commanded Your Servant [Qian] Xili 錢習禮 and Your Servant [Chen] Yu 陳愉 to go and preside over the affair. On the renzi day, the examination compound was locked; on the guichou, bingchen, and jiwei days, examination questions were issued three times in all. When the thorny barriers were removed, one hundred and fifty men whose essays were of superior grade were obtained. Now that the examination record has been completed, Your Servant Yu respectfully writes a postface at its end. I humbly reflect that a scholar cultivates himself at home and is nurtured…

punctuated: 於學，朝夕涵泳，培植性情，啟迪志慮，必以德行道藝為本；而科目之取，必試之以文詞者，蓋德行道藝蘊於心，欲見諸事為之著，非言焉不足以發之。文則言之成章者也。然文必以理為主，然後見其學之正、言之純，庶乎其道德之文，匪徒為馳騁妍麗、緣飾藻繪而已。諸士子生逢全盛之日，大音正完，而能以文得儁，登名茲錄，藹乎其德義之發，行將奉清問、膺寵命、列官顯要，尚其以是言體諸身、
translation_en: …in schools—immersing themselves day and night, cultivating their dispositions and feelings, and inspiring their aspirations and thoughts—must take moral conduct and the Dao and the arts as their foundation. Yet when selecting through the examination categories, we must test them by means of literary compositions. This is because moral conduct and the Dao and the arts are stored within the mind; if one wishes to see them manifested in deeds and actions, without words there is no sufficient means to bring them forth. Literature is speech brought into patterned form. However, literature must take principle as its master; only then can one see the correctness of a scholar's learning and the purity of his words. Thus it may approximate the literature of morality and virtue, rather than merely galloping in beauty and elegance or embellishing with ornate rhetoric. You scholars have been born into an era of complete flourishing, when the great tone is in full perfection, and you have been able through your writing to distinguish yourselves and have your names entered into this record, abundant in the manifestation of your virtue and righteousness. Soon you will receive the Emperor's pure inquiry, accept his favored mandate, and take your places in prominent and important offices. May you embody these words in your own persons…

翰林院侍講學士奉直大夫馬愉謹序。
translation_en:
…and put them into practice in affairs; look up and reflect upon how the worthies and sages of antiquity established their minds and regulated their conduct; plan for what is far-reaching and great; bestow benefits to nourish the common people; assist in furthering the Sacred Transformation; and thereby proclaim the flourishing of the Dynasty—all the more sufficing to show that what they have learned ultimately leads to uprightness, greatness, and lofty illumination. It is my wish that we mutually encourage one another in this.
Respectfully prefaced by Ma Yu 馬愉, Hanlin Academician Expositor-in-waiting and Grand Master for Fostering Uprightness.
